quran-affirms-torah-gospel.claim: The Quran treats the Torah and Gospel of Muhammad's own day as real, present and authoritative. It 'confirms what came before it' (Quran 3:3). It asks why Jews come to Muhammad for judgment 'while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah' (5:43) — with them, in the present tense. It commands 'the People of the Gospel' to 'judge by what Allah has revealed therein' (5:46-47). It tells Jews and Christians they are 'on nothing' until they uphold the Torah and Gospel (5:68). It tells Muhammad himself, if in doubt, to 'ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you' (10:94). And it declares that 'none can alter His words' (6:115; 18:27). A corrupted, unreliable Bible cannot be what any of those verses mean. So the tahrif, or corruption, doctrine faces a fork. Corruption before Muhammad contradicts the Quran. Corruption after Muhammad is ruled out by surviving manuscripts.
quran-affirms-torah-gospel.response: IslamQA gives the mainstream answer. The Quran confirms the original revealed Torah and Injil. By Muhammad's time the circulating texts had already been altered in places. They were corrupted here and there, yet still held truth. That is why the Quran can appeal to what remains without endorsing the whole. A second line argues that the Injil is a distinct revelation given to Jesus, not the four Gospels Christians possess. On this account affirmation and corruption sit together: the Quran affirms what is genuinely from Allah in their books, and corrects the rest.
quran-affirms-torah-gospel.rationale: The 'already corrupted by Muhammad's day' answer collides with the plain sense of the verses. Quran 5:43 says the Torah with them contains Allah's judgment now. Quran 5:47 commands present-tense judgment by the Gospel. Quran 10:94 makes readers of the earlier Scripture the check on Muhammad's own revelation. None of that is coherent if those texts were unreliable. The 'lost original Injil' answer posits a book with no historical or manuscript existence at all, and 5:47 addresses the actual People of the Gospel and what they hold. Neither horn is escaped. The answers move the problem rather than resolve it.

tahrif-doctrine-late-development.claim: The charge that the Bible's text was falsified — tahrif al-nass — is not the Quran's teaching, and it was not early Islam's. Gordon Nickel studied the earliest Quran commentaries, including Muqatil ibn Sulayman in the 8th century and al-Tabari, who died in 923. They understood the tampering verses as misinterpretation, concealment and mispronunciation by Jews and Christians. That is tahrif al-mana, corruption of meaning, not of text. Ibn Abbas, cited in Sahih al-Bukhari's Book of Tawhid, said no one can remove the words of Allah from His books; people distort meanings by misreading. The full text-corruption doctrine only crystallised with Ibn Hazm of Cordoba, who died in 1064 — four centuries after Muhammad. It hardened as a polemical necessity once the differences between Bible and Quran were pressed.
tahrif-doctrine-late-development.response: Muslim apologists reply that tahrif al-nass is no medieval invention. The Quran says 'a party of them used to hear the words of Allah and then distort it' (2:75). It condemns 'those who write the Book with their own hands, then say: this is from Allah' (2:79) — physical writing, not mere misreading. They also note that the same Ibn Abbas, in Sahih al-Bukhari 7363, says the People of the Book 'changed and altered' their Book and wrote it with their own hands. So the early testimony cuts both ways. On this view Ibn Hazm systematised the doctrine rather than inventing it. Islamweb argues the same in its fatwa on judging by the Torah and Gospel.
tahrif-doctrine-late-development.rationale: The load-bearing facts are conceded inside Islamic sources and in academic scholarship. The earliest exegetes overwhelmingly read the tampering verses as distortion of meaning. Bukhari preserves Ibn Abbas denying that anyone can change Allah's words in His books. Even reviewers sympathetic to Islam grant that only Ibn Hazm and al-Maqdisi held thoroughgoing textual corruption among the classical authorities. Quran 2:79 addresses a party writing false material and selling it. It never says the Torah's manuscript tradition was rewritten, and no early source identifies when, where or by whom that global rewrite happened. The doctrine every dawah presentation depends on is historically late.

manuscripts-predate-muhammad.claim: Whatever text the Quran affirmed in Muhammad's day, between 610 and 632 AD, is recoverable — and it is the same in substance as today's Bible. The Dead Sea Scrolls date from about 250 BC to 70 AD. They include the complete Great Isaiah Scroll, from about 125 BC, with Isaiah 53 intact, and they substantially match the Masoretic text behind modern Old Testaments. The Septuagint translation dates to the 3rd and 2nd centuries BC. Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, from the mid-4th century AD, each contain the complete New Testament or nearly so, and they are the base of modern critical editions. They predate Muhammad by about 250 years. So the second horn is sealed: no corruption after Muhammad is possible, because the text from before him survives, and it is our text.
manuscripts-predate-muhammad.response: The strongest Muslim reply concedes the manuscripts and redirects. Textual stability since 600 AD is beside the point, because the corruption alleged is older than any of these witnesses. The originals of Moses and Jesus were lost or altered in the centuries before Qumran and Sinaiticus. So today's Bible faithfully transmits a text that had already gone wrong. IslamQA adds two supports. The Dead Sea Scrolls themselves show textual plurality, with variant editions of Jeremiah and Samuel. And the New Testament critical apparatus records hundreds of thousands of variants. That proves the transmission was human and fallible, not divinely guarded as the Quran's is claimed to be.
manuscripts-predate-muhammad.rationale: The redirect impales itself on the first horn. If the Bible was already corrupt centuries before Muhammad, then the Quran's commands to judge by it, its claim that the Torah 'with them' contains Allah's judgment, and its instruction to resolve doubt by asking its readers are all commendations of a corrupt book. The variant-plurality point is a category error. No Dead Sea Scroll and no New Testament variant tradition removes the crucifixion, the resurrection or divine sonship — the things the Quran needs absent. Those are textually secure across every manuscript stream. The manuscripts leave no window in which the required wholesale corruption could have happened.

crucifixion-denial-vs-history.claim: Quran 4:157 says of the Jews: 'they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but another was made to resemble him to them.' That is a single verse, composed about 600 years after the event and more than a thousand kilometres away. All four gospels report the event. So does a pre-Pauline creed dated to within a few years of it (1 Corinthians 15:3-8). So do two non-Christian historians: Josephus (Antiquities 18.3.3) and Tacitus (Annals 15.44). Critical historians across the spectrum treat it as bedrock. Bart Ehrman, an agnostic, writes: 'One of the most certain facts of history is that Jesus was crucified on orders of the Roman prefect of Judea, Pontius Pilate.' Gerd Lüdemann, an atheist, writes: 'The fact of the death of Jesus as a consequence of crucifixion is indisputable.' No case for the denial rests on historical method. It rests only on the Quran's authority.
crucifixion-denial-vs-history.response: The classical Sunni answer is substitution. Allah cast Jesus's likeness onto another — Judas, Simon of Cyrene, or a volunteer disciple, depending on the tafsir. That man was crucified while Allah raised Jesus alive (4:158). 'It was made to appear so to them' explains exactly why every observer, and so every historical record, honestly reports a crucifixion. A miracle escapes historical method by definition. The Ahmadiyya hold instead that Jesus survived the cross. And a minority scholarly stream, documented by Todd Lawson and argued by Mahmoud Ayoub, reads 4:157 as denying only the Jews' boast of agency: they did not kill him, God's plan prevailed. On that reading the event itself is left neither affirmed nor denied.
crucifixion-denial-vs-history.rationale: Substitution cannot be falsified, by design. It concedes all the evidence and overrides it with an unwitnessed miracle attested six centuries later. That is an abandonment of historical argument, not an answer to one. It also makes God the author of the deception that founded Christianity. The Lawson and Ayoub reading is the strongest move, because it stops denying the event. But it rescues the Quran by surrendering the traditional Islamic claim. Read traditionally, 4:157 stands against the strongest evidence set in ancient history. There is no counter-evidence at all.

quran-jesus-resume.claim: The Quran gives Jesus a profile it gives no one else, including Muhammad. He is virgin-born (3:47). He is 'the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter' (3:45). He is announced as 'a pure boy', that is, sinless (19:19). He works miracles, healing the blind and the leper and raising the dead (3:49; 5:110). He never dies; 'Allah raised him to Himself', so he is alive in heaven now (4:158). In Islamic eschatology he returns at the end of the age (Sahih al-Bukhari 3448). Muhammad, by contrast, is commanded to 'ask forgiveness for your sin' (47:19; 48:2), performs no miracle in the Quran, and is dead in Medina. Every data point the Quran itself supplies points to Jesus's uniqueness — and then forbids the conclusion they suggest.
quran-jesus-resume.response: The Quran heads off the inference itself: 'The example of Jesus with Allah is like that of Adam; He created him from dust, then said to him: Be, and he was' (3:59). A fatherless origin proves creative sovereignty, not divinity — otherwise Adam, who had no father and no mother, would be more divine still. Omar Suleiman of the Yaqeen Institute develops this reading. Every miracle in 3:49 carries the refrain bi-idhnillah, 'by Allah's permission', marking Jesus as an empowered servant rather than a source. His sinlessness and his ascension are honours Allah bestows on whom He wills, and prophets differ in gifts (2:253) without differing in nature. Jesus's greatness is affirmed exactly as the second greatest of servants — never as God's son, a title he himself will disown (5:116-117).
quran-jesus-resume.rationale: The Adam analogy and the bi-idhnillah refrain are genuine, coherent answers to the virgin birth and the miracles taken one at a time. This is Islam's best-drilled ground. But the analogy covers origin only. Adam sinned. Jesus is the only figure the Quran calls pure. He is never shown sinning, never recorded dying, and is titled al-Masih without that title ever being defined. He is stationed alive in heaven pending his return — while the Quran's final prophet is twice told to seek forgiveness for his sin. The cumulative asymmetry is unanswered as a whole, even though every part has a rehearsed reply. That is why this is contested rather than unrefuted, and a door-opener rather than a defeater.

gospel-judgment-test.claim: The Quran creates a verification procedure and then fails it. Quran 10:94 tells Muhammad: 'If you are in doubt about what We have revealed to you, then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you.' The Scripture-readers are the arbiters. Quran 5:47 commands: 'Let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed therein', with a warning that whoever does not judge by it is 'defiantly disobedient'. Now run the test. The Gospel possessed by every People of the Gospel community in 632 AD was the fourfold Gospel, its text secured by Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus two centuries earlier. Judging by that Gospel, as commanded, returns the verdict that Jesus was crucified, rose, and is the divine Son — a verdict against the book that issued the command.
gospel-judgment-test.response: Classical tafsir handles both verses. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read 10:94 as rhetorical: the address is formally to Muhammad but is really aimed at doubters. The ones to ask are the honest scholars of the Book, such as Abdullah ibn Salam, who recognised Muhammad foretold in their texts — not Christians at large on matters of doctrine. On 5:47, Islamweb fatwa 92519 argues the command is to judge by what Allah actually revealed in the Injil. That means the authentic core, including Muhammad's description and God's law, not every doctrine the church later layered on top. A command to use a book's genuine content is not an endorsement of its corruptions. And the Injil of the Quran is the revelation given to Jesus, not the four biographical Gospels written by others.
gospel-judgment-test.rationale: Each escape is circular. 'Ask only those who converted' filters the arbiters by agreement with the conclusion, which guts 10:94 as a test; the verse names no such filter and assumes the consulted Scripture is reliable. 'Judge by the authentic core' requires a criterion for which Gospel content is authentic, and the only criterion offered is agreement with the Quran — the book under test. And the 'real Injil' is historically empty. No 7th-century community called 'People of the Gospel' possessed any book but the fourfold Gospel. So 5:47's command has no possible referent except the text that refutes the Quran's Christology. The test stands as designed, and the Quran fails it.

uthman-burning-companion-codices.claim: The contrast between a perfectly preserved Quran and a corrupted Bible fails on Islam's own sources. Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 records that within about twenty years of Muhammad's death Muslims were 'differing about the Quran as the Jews and Christians differed about their Scripture'. So Caliph Uthman had one recension copied and ordered all other Quranic material, 'whether written in fragmentary manuscripts or whole copies, be burnt'. Companion codices differed. Early Islamic sources report that Ibn Masud's codex lacked Surahs 1, 113 and 114, and Bukhari 4977 preserves the dispute, while Ubayy ibn Ka'b's contained two extra surahs. Bukhari 4992 shows companions disputing recitations in Muhammad's own lifetime, resolved by the 'seven ahruf' concession. A text preserved by destroying its variant witnesses cannot indict the Bible for having variant witnesses that survived.
uthman-burning-companion-codices.response: The best Muslim scholarship, from Al-Azami and the Yaqeen Institute, argues this proves preservation rather than corruption. The Quran was revealed in seven ahruf, or modes, all divinely authorised, so companion differences were sanctioned variation and not error. Uthman's standardisation was done by a committee of memorisers cross-checking against Hafsa's master copy, with community consensus, and it eliminated only unauthorised or abrogated readings before drift could set in. That is the opposite of the Bible's uncontrolled copying. Living mass memorisation, tawatur, carried the text alongside the writing. And Yaqeen's analysis finds that fewer than 4% of variant readings attributed to companions even have authentic chains.
uthman-burning-companion-codices.rationale: Every fact in the claim sits in Sahih al-Bukhari itself — the differing recitations, the burning order, the companion codex disputes. So the events are conceded, and only their interpretation is defended. The ahruf framework is a theological explanation, not a historical control. The ahruf themselves are undefined in the sources, the burned material is unrecoverable by design, and 'the variants were all authorised' cannot be tested once the witnesses are ash. The narrow point survives every response. The Quran's uniformity is the product of a documented 7th-century editorial intervention, which forfeits the dawah contrast with a Bible whose variant manuscripts were preserved and can be openly compared.

sanaa-palimpsest-qiraat.claim: Physical and living evidence confirms that the Quran has textual plurality. The Sanaa palimpsest was found in 1972 in the Great Mosque of Sanaa, and its parchment is radiocarbon-dated to the 7th century. Its lower, erased text differs from the Uthmanic standard in wording and surah order. It is the only surviving non-Uthmanic text tradition, and it matches the reports of companion codices. Today the Quran is printed in multiple canonical readings, the qira'at. The Hafs text is used by most of the world; the Warsh text is used across North and West Africa. They differ in hundreds of places, mostly minor, but some changing meaning — Quran 3:146 reads qatala, 'fought', or qutila, 'was killed'. Keith Small's manuscript study concludes that an early edited form of the consonantal text is recoverable, but the original forms of the text are not. 'Not one dot has changed' is a dawah slogan, not a manuscript finding.
sanaa-palimpsest-qiraat.response: The Yaqeen Institute treatment by Khatib and Khan, and Al-Azami's History of the Qur'anic Text, answer that the qira'at are not variants in the Western text-critical sense. They are parallel revealed recitations within the ahruf. All were mass-transmitted from the Prophet. All fit the Uthmanic skeleton, and all are doctrinally identical. Differences like qatala and qutila enrich meaning without contradiction. Bible variants can affect whole passages, such as Mark 16 and John 7:53-8:11. The Sanaa lower text is explained as a companion's personal or pre-canonical copy, properly washed and superseded. That shows the community enforcing the standard exactly as the preservation promise in 15:9 implies.
sanaa-palimpsest-qiraat.rationale: Honest grading cuts both ways. Against the dawah slogan the claim wins: multiple printed texts with real wording differences exist today, the Sanaa lower text is a physically extant non-Uthmanic Quran, and academic study confirms early editing. So 'letter-perfect, unlike the Bible' is false as stated. But against academic standards the Quran's transmission is genuinely tight. Behnam Sadeghi published the Sanaa findings with Mohsen Goudarzi in 2012. He himself argues that the Uthmanic text substantially reflects the Prophet's recitation. And the qira'at differences are far smaller than the rhetoric suggests. The double standard is exposed; wholesale corruption of the Quran is not shown. Use this entry to level the playing field, not to mirror the dawah overclaim in reverse.

trinity-father-jesus-mary.claim: Quran 5:116 has Allah interrogate Jesus: 'Did you say to people, take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?' It is the only place the Quran names the members of the godhead it rejects. It names Mary, not the Holy Spirit. No orthodox Christian creed, East or West, ever included Mary in the Trinity. The critique runs like this. An all-knowing author would refute what the Nicene church confessed: one Being, three Persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Refuting a triad that includes Mary instead looks like a human author reflecting garbled or folk Christianity in 7th-century Arabia. Quran 5:75 points the same way, arguing that Jesus and Mary 'both ate food', which pairs them as the two venerated creatures.
trinity-father-jesus-mary.response: There are two levels to the answer, and the second is stronger. The popular one says the verse addresses a real heresy: Epiphanius, who died in 403, describes the Collyridians, Arabian women who offered cakes to Mary as a goddess. On that reading the Quran corrects them, not Nicaea. The academic answer, used by Gabriel Said Reynolds, Sidney Griffith, Mun'im Sirry and David Thomas, is that 5:116 is not a doctrinal report at all. It is eschatological rhetoric. It warns against the drift toward excessive veneration of Jesus and Mary. That drift was visible in icons and in 'Theotokos' devotion. It gives examples of shirk rather than defining the Trinity.
trinity-father-jesus-mary.rationale: The rhetorical-warning reading is a genuine steelman with mainstream academic backing, so 'strawman, full stop' overclaims. But that steelman has costs Muslims rarely price in. There is no evidence the Collyridians existed in 7th-century Hijaz; the sect is attested once, 250 years earlier. Much of the classical tafsir tradition read 5:116 as what Christians actually believed, so the rhetoric-only reading is partly a modern retreat. And even granting the rhetoric, one gap remains. The Quran nowhere states the actual formula — Father, Son and Spirit, one essence — in order to refute it. A book claiming divine omniscience, sent to correct Christians, never once describes correctly the doctrine it condemns. That silence is the enduring point.

trinity-third-of-three.claim: Quran 5:73 condemns those who say 'Allah is the third of three' — thalithu thalatha — and 4:171 commands 'do not say Three'. Orthodox Trinitarian teaching has never asserted that God is one of three gods. The Athanasian formula is explicit: 'not three Gods, but one God'. 'Third of three' describes tritheism, a position the church condemns as heresy. So the Quran anathematises a numerical polytheism that Christians also anathematise, while never engaging the actual claim: one divine Being eternally existing as three Persons.
trinity-third-of-three.response: The strongest reply has three parts. First, 'third of three' may render Syriac Christian usage. Sidney Griffith notes that some Syriac texts call Christ thlithaya, one of three, so the Quran may echo actual Arabic-Christian speech rather than misdescribe the doctrine. Second, whatever the creeds say, worshipping three distinct persons is in practice indistinguishable from three gods; IslamQA 243142 refuses the metaphysical fine print and rejects the arithmetic at its root. Third, Shabir Ally argues the verse targets what ordinary Christians effectively believed, and that the 'one essence' defence is philosophically incoherent anyway, so refuting 'three' is sufficient.
trinity-third-of-three.rationale: If 'third of three' echoes a Syriac title of Christ, the phrase has a defensible pedigree, and 'your maths is still three' is a coherent if blunt polemical stance. But the Muslim defence concedes the core observation. The Quran refutes the Trinity only in a form Christians themselves anathematise, and never once states the actual claim in order to answer it. The Christian can fairly say: my belief has never been addressed by the Quran, only a caricature adjacent to it. The 'deliberate simplification' defence is possible but unevidenced, and it is equally consistent with an author who knew Christianity only through popular report.

begets-consort-carnal-sonship.claim: Surah 112:3 says God 'neither begets nor is born', and Quran 6:101 asks 'How can He have a son when He has no consort?' Both attack divine sonship as though it required a female partner and sexual procreation. But the Nicene Creed of 325 AD, three centuries before the Quran, had already defined the Son as 'begotten, not made' — eternal generation within the one divine essence, explicitly not carnal. Christians agree that God has no consort and no physical offspring. The Quran's rhetorical question therefore lands only against pagan carnal sonship. That is evidence its author knew the pagan Arab concept of Allah's 'daughters' (53:19-21) but not the Christian doctrine it claims to refute.
begets-consort-carnal-sonship.response: The strongest reply has three parts. First, most of the Quran's sonship denials use walad, meaning biological offspring — precisely the carnal notion. The target is pagan Arabs who gave Allah daughters. The context of 6:100 is Meccan polytheists. It also covers any Christian who slid toward literalism. Second, al-Tabari reads 6:101 as a reductio against pagan genealogy for God. Third, on Muslim analysis 'eternal generation' is itself an incoherent evasion: 'begotten' either means dependency and origination, and so creaturehood, or it is empty honorific language. Either way tawhid stands, and the denial in 19:92 covers every version of sonship.
begets-consort-carnal-sonship.rationale: The context-is-pagans defence for 6:101 is textually respectable, and Christians do deny carnal begetting, so the verses may pass each other rather than collide. But Surah 112 and 2:116 are traditionally read against Christians too, and the Quran's only stated argument against divine sonship is the missing consort. It adds only that sonship is unbefitting. It never engages eternal generation, the Christian position for 300 years. The criticism is not that the Quran affirms something false. It is that it argues against the doctrine's crudest counterfeit and declares victory. This stays contested, because a Muslim can claim the denial was meant to cover everything. But that reading makes the consort argument a non sequitur. It would then answer no Christian who actually existed.

god-is-love-monad.claim: 1 John 4:8 makes love God's essence: 'God is love'. Love is inherently other-directed — lover, beloved, love. The Trinity grounds that eternally, since the Father loves the Son 'before the foundation of the world' (John 17:24). A unitarian monad, by contrast, had no one to love before creation. So either love is not essential to Allah, and he became loving when he made creatures, or he was eternally self-focused. There is a corollary. 'Father' is not among the 99 names, and Allah is never called Father in the Quran. Love in the Quran is predominantly conditional — 'Allah loves those who...' and 'Allah loves not the transgressors' (2:190; 3:31-32) — while 5:18 rebukes Jews and Christians for calling themselves children of Allah.
god-is-love-monad.response: The reply has three parts. First, al-Wadud, 'the Most Loving', appears twice (11:90; 85:14), so divine love is a real Quranic attribute, and Sahih Muslim 2751a says His mercy prevails over His wrath; the claim that Islam's God lacks love is simply false. Second, Abdullah al Andalusi's rebuttal to William Lane Craig: an attribute can be eternal as a disposition without being eternally exercised. Allah is eternally al-Khaliq, Creator, without an eternal creation, so likewise eternally loving without an eternal beloved. Demanding eternal actualisation proves too much, since it would require an eternal object of mercy and wrath as well. Third, Bassam Zawadi and al Andalusi argue that Craig's definition of perfect love as self-giving to another person begs the question in favour of Trinitarianism.
god-is-love-monad.rationale: This is philosophical theology, not documentary fact, and both sides have live moves. The Christian argument has real force. In the Quran love is never predicated of God's essence — 'Allah is love' appears nowhere — it is characteristically conditional on obedience (3:31), and 'Father', the Bible's central relational name, is absent and its use denied (5:18). But the disposition-versus-actualisation distinction is a serious answer that Craig's argument must work to defeat. The honest grade splits the claim. The comparative textual point holds: the Bible makes love essential and eternally actual in a way the Quran does not. The philosophical point, that a monad cannot be perfectly loving, is contested.

best-of-deceivers.claim: Quran 3:54 and 8:30 call Allah khayru al-makirin. The root m-k-r denotes scheming, guile and deception in the classical Arabic lexicons Lane and Lisan al-Arab. Quran 3:54 sits in exactly the crucifixion context: Allah's makr answers the makr of others, and 4:157's 'it was made to appear so to them' is the payoff — a mass deception that produced what Islam calls Christianity's central error. The Bible asserts the opposite of God: he 'cannot lie' (Titus 1:2; Numbers 23:19; Hebrews 6:18). If the biggest deception in salvation history, a faked crucifixion, is Allah's own makr, then the character of Islam's God differs fundamentally from the Bible's.
best-of-deceivers.response: Islamweb fatwa 295183, and treatments citing Jamal Badawi, answer on three fronts. First, makr means a hidden stratagem and is morally neutral in itself; its value depends on its object. Allah's makr is always retributive, out-planning plotters to protect the innocent — here, saving Jesus from murder. So 'best of planners' is ethics, not euphemism. Second, Quranic usage of makr for Allah is always responsive to human makr (3:54; 8:30; 10:21), never initiated against the sincere. Third, there is a tu quoque with teeth: the Bible has God sending 'a lying spirit' (1 Kings 22:22-23), 'a strong delusion so they believe the lie' (2 Thessalonians 2:11), and deceiving prophets (Ezekiel 14:9). If makr indicts Allah, those indict Yahweh.
best-of-deceivers.rationale: Lexically the critics are on firm ground. Makr is consistently negative of humans in the Quran itself, including 'evil makr' in 35:43, and sanitised translations like 'best of planners' are apologetically motivated. But the theological indictment is weaker than the lexical point. Retributive counter-scheming is defensible divine behaviour, and the biblical counter-texts show that Christians must themselves distinguish judicial deception of the wicked from essential untruthfulness. Where the argument keeps its bite is 4:157. On mainstream tafsir, Allah's stratagem produced a false appearance that deceived Jesus's own sincere followers, founding six centuries of what Islam calls error. That is a judicial deception of the sincere, which the biblical parallels do not match. It is strongest as a companion to the crucifixion-denial entry.

word-and-spirit-titles.claim: Quran 4:171 calls Jesus 'the Messenger of Allah and His Word (kalimatuhu) which He cast to Mary, and a Spirit from Him (ruhun minhu).' These titles are given to no other figure in the Quran, not even to Muhammad. Sahih al-Bukhari 3286 adds that every newborn is touched by Satan except Mary and her son. So the Quran's own Christology keeps gesturing above prophet-rank. Word, Spirit, sinless, virgin-born, alive in heaven, returning. It echoes the language of John 1, where the Word became flesh, in the very act of denying what John says about him.
word-and-spirit-titles.response: The strongest reply comes from the tafsir tradition itself, in Ibn Kathir, Jalalayn and Maududi. 'His Word' means that Jesus was created by Allah's word 'Be', kun. Quran 3:59 makes this explicit and levels him with Adam, who had neither father nor mother. A miraculous origin proves creaturehood, not divinity. 'A spirit from Him' uses the preposition min, which marks origin rather than shared being; Quran 45:13 uses 'from Him' of everything. The titles sit under the verse's own stated ceiling: 'the Messiah is only a messenger... do not say Three.' On this reading the verse borrows Christian vocabulary precisely in order to deflate it.
word-and-spirit-titles.rationale: The Muslim reading is internally coherent, and Quran 3:59 supplies the Quran's own gloss. But it under-explains the data. Everything is created by 'Be' (2:117), yet only Jesus is called 'His Word'. The Adam parallel also cuts against the no-consort argument of 6:101, since a miraculous fatherless origin is apparently fine when Allah wills it. And the cumulative profile is one the Quran never paints of Muhammad. What the Quran inherits here is Johannine vocabulary, the Logos, stripped of the theology that produced it. That is what borrowing from a Christian setting without its doctrinal grammar looks like. There is no formal contradiction, but there is a standing tension resolved only by stipulation.

clay-birds-apocrypha.claim: The Quran's two signature Jesus miracles are absent from the canonical gospels, and both have documented literary ancestors in Christian apocrypha. The child Jesus forming birds from clay and breathing life into them (3:49; 5:110) parallels the Infancy Gospel of Thomas 2:1-5, a Greek text of the mid-2nd century — a legend cycle in which the boy Jesus also strikes playmates dead. Jesus speaking from the cradle (19:29-33; 3:46) parallels the Arabic Infancy Gospel, a Syriac-derived compilation of the 5th or 6th century, where the infant says 'I am the Son of God'. Both texts predate the Quran by centuries and circulated in Syriac and Arabic Christian settings. So the Quran presents legendary material composed 100 to 500 years after Jesus as historical revelation. That is exactly what a 7th-century author absorbing local Christian folklore would produce.
clay-birds-apocrypha.response: Islamweb fatwa 367270 answers on three fronts. First, a parallel is not dependence. A shared story may mean the apocryphon preserved a genuine event the canonical gospels omitted, since John 21:25 admits Jesus did many unrecorded things. The Quran, as revelation, confirms the true kernel and corrects the legend's distortions — adding 'by Allah's leave' to guard tawhid and dropping the morally troubling elements. Second, the direction of correction is telling, since random borrowing would not sanitise. Third, some Muslim writers embrace the parallel as vindication: an unlettered Meccan trader could not have accessed Greek or Syriac apocrypha, so agreement with ancient Christian tradition is evidence of revelation.
clay-birds-apocrypha.rationale: All parties concede the parallels. Only the direction is debated. The 'apocrypha preserved real events' defence cannot be falsified and carries no evidence: no historian treats the Infancy Gospel of Thomas or the Arabic Infancy Gospel as history. The cradle speech even carries its source's fingerprint. In the Arabic Infancy Gospel the infant says 'I am the Son of God'; in the Quran the same scene is repurposed to say the opposite. The 'unlettered trader' argument fails on the texts' known circulation in Syriac Christian Arabia and on oral transmission. The Quran itself records the accusation that Muhammad heard 'tales of the ancients dictated morning and evening' (25:4-5). Mainstream scholarship's sober conclusion stands: the Quran retells late Christian folklore as fact.

son-of-god-divine-claims.claim: The Quran attacks a 'Son of God' its opponents never held, meaning physical offspring, while the actual biblical claim goes unaddressed. 'Son of God' is a royal and divine title (Psalm 2:7), and in Jesus's usage it asserted equality with God. John 5:18 says the Jews sought to kill him because 'he was even calling God his own Father, making himself equal with God'. Consider his own claims. 'Before Abraham was, I am' (John 8:58), met with an attempted stoning. Mark 14:61-64: 'I am, and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven' — the language of Daniel 7 — ruled capital blasphemy. John 20:28: Thomas says 'My Lord and my God', and is blessed, not rebuked. Every one of these texts exists in manuscripts predating Islam by 200 to 450 years — P66 and P75 from about 200 AD, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus from the 4th century. Whatever one thinks of their truth, the claims demonstrably predate the Quran's denial of them.
son-of-god-divine-claims.response: The strongest reply, argued by Shabir Ally and Bassam Zawadi, has five parts. First, 'Son of God' is demonstrably metaphorical throughout the Bible — Adam (Luke 3:38), Israel (Exodus 4:22), David at his coronation (Psalm 2:7), peacemakers (Matthew 5:9). Second, John 8:58's ego eimi is not the divine name: the Greek Exodus 3:14 renders the name as ho on, and the healed blind man says ego eimi in John 9:9. Third, the strongest claims cluster in John, the latest gospel, reflecting developed church theology — the Synoptic Jesus prays, calls the Father 'the only true God' (John 17:3), and disclaims omniscience (Mark 13:32). Fourth, Mark 14:62's exaltation claim is one a Jewish agent of God could make, and blasphemy verdicts were elastic. Fifth, Jesus never says 'I am God; worship me.'
son-of-god-divine-claims.rationale: The historical-critical retreat, that John is late theology, is a real argument with academic support. But it is Pyrrhic for a Muslim. It concedes that the gospels say what Christians say they say, and it rescues Islam only by adopting a source-critical scepticism the Quran never licenses — since the Quran tells Christians to judge by their Gospel (5:47). The narrower rebuttals are weak. The ego-eimi deflation ignores the immediate stoning attempt (8:59) and the absolute construction. The Mark 14 deflation must explain a capital blasphemy verdict. John 20:28 has no deflationary reading, since 'my Lord and my God' is addressed to Jesus, who blesses rather than corrects. And the manuscript point is untouched: the divine claims predate Islam in surviving physical copies. Contested, but leaning heavily against the Muslim position on the documentary question.

quran-never-quotes-scriptures.claim: The Quran claims to confirm, musaddiq, the Torah and Gospel (2:97; 3:3; 5:48; 46:12). Yet in 6,236 verses it contains essentially no verbatim quotation of the texts it confirms. The single near-exception is 21:105: 'We wrote in the Zabur... My righteous servants shall inherit the earth', which corresponds to Psalm 37:29. Its biblical narratives arrive garbled through midrash and apocrypha — Cain's raven from Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer (5:31), Abraham in the fiery furnace from midrash (21:68-69), Mary confused with Miriam sister of Aaron (19:28). Contrast the New Testament, which quotes the Old Testament about 300 times, explicitly. That is what confirming previous scripture looks like. Sidney Griffith's scholarship confirms that no written Arabic Bible existed before Islam. The Quran's biblical knowledge is oral and homiletic, which fits Muhammad's documented contacts — Waraqa ibn Nawfal, Khadija's Christian cousin, who 'used to write the Gospel in Arabic' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3) — and the accusation recorded in 25:4-5.
quran-never-quotes-scriptures.response: Islamweb fatwa 367270 and Ibn Kathir on 3:3 answer in four parts. First, the Quran is not a commentary but a fresh revelation from the same source. Musaddiq means it confirms the previous revelations' divine origin and core message — tawhid, judgment, the prophets — not their surviving letter, so quotation is neither promised nor needed. Second, it does engage biblical content: 21:105 quotes the Psalms by name and gets it right, 7:157 says Muhammad is 'written with them in the Torah and the Gospel', and 48:29 paraphrases the seed parable as 'its likeness in the Gospel'. Third, arguing from silence is weak, since the audience was largely pagan Meccans and extended quotation of texts unavailable in Arabic would serve no purpose. Fourth, retelling with variation is the Quran's stated method (12:3), so divergence from midrash-contaminated tellings is correction, not error.
quran-never-quotes-scriptures.rationale: The core datum is undisputed. There are no verbatim quotations of Torah or Gospel text in the entire Quran, and one loose Psalm citation. The responses explain why that might be acceptable; none disputes that it is so. And the explanations strain against the Quran's own posture. It stakes its authenticity on continuity with prior scripture (10:94; 5:47), yet shows no direct acquaintance with either text, while showing detailed acquaintance with post-biblical legend. The 7:157 counter-example sharpens the problem: the Quran asserts that Muhammad is written in books it never quotes, and fourteen centuries of apologetics has not produced the passage. Griffith's finding is the naturalistic explanation sitting in plain sight.

injil-problem.claim: The Quran speaks of 'the Injil' as a single book Allah gave to Jesus (5:46; 57:27), which mainstream Islam says was later lost or corrupted, leaving the four gospels as unreliable human residue. There are two problems. First, no trace of any such book exists — no manuscript, no fragment, no citation by any ancient author, friend or enemy, in the seven centuries between Jesus and Muhammad. From the earliest records 'gospel', euangelion, was the proclamation about Jesus, and the written gospels are biographies about him. That is a category the Quran appears to misunderstand. Second, the Quran forecloses the lost-book escape itself. Quran 5:47 commands 'let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed in it' — a present-tense command in 610 to 632 AD, presupposing an Injil then in Christian hands. Demonstrably that was the four gospels, complete in 4th-century codices. Either those gospels were trustworthy, and Islam's Christology is falsified by them, or they were corrupt, and Allah commanded people to judge by a corrupted book he was simultaneously confirming.
injil-problem.response: There are two lines, and they are incompatible with each other. The mainstream one, from IslamQA, holds that the original Injil was Allah's verbal revelation to Jesus, transmitted in his preaching. It survives partly within the four gospels but entangled with human narrative, which is tahrif. Quran 5:47 then commands Christians to judge by what remains of the genuine revelation inside their books. The absence of a separate manuscript is expected, since it was lost early, and that is the whole reason the Quran was sent. The revisionist line, argued by V. A. Mohamad Ashrof and other modernists, concedes that the lost-book thesis is a myth. On that view the Quran's Injil simply is the gospel possessed by 7th-century Christians, treated as containing genuine revelation. The corruption verses then target misinterpretation and concealment rather than textual loss. Gordon Nickel's work on the early tafsir supports that reading.
injil-problem.rationale: The dilemma survives because the two Muslim answers refute each other. The 'lost original' view has literally no historical evidence. No source in any century attests a revealed book given to Jesus; it is an anachronism projected backward from the Quran's assumption that every prophet receives a book. The revisionist view fits the Quranic data far better and has early-tafsir support. But it pays for that by authenticating the four gospels Christians actually held in 610 AD, whose text is fixed by 4th-century codices, and which teach the incarnation, crucifixion and resurrection the Quran denies. There is no third option. Fourteen centuries in, no Muslim can produce, describe, date or quote the 'real Injil'. This is arguably the sharpest internal-consistency problem in the Quran's engagement with Christianity.

sun-muddy-spring.claim: Quran 18:86 says Dhul-Qarnayn travelled until 'he reached the setting-place of the sun; he found it setting in a muddy spring'. The parallel at 18:90 gives a literal rising-place, where the sun rises on a people with no shelter from it. Early tafsir shows this was understood literally. Al-Tabari preserves narrations taking the sun as actually setting in the spring, and Ibn Kathir describes 'a blackened, muddy and stinking spring'. A supporting hadith exists in Sunan Abi Dawud 4002: 'It sets in a spring of warm water.' Albani graded its chain sahih, though some scholars argue the 'spring' wording is the narrator's description rather than the Prophet's. Either way, the tafsir record independently evidences a literal cosmology.
sun-muddy-spring.response: IslamQA 176375 answers that the verse describes what Dhul-Qarnayn perceived from his vantage point. 'He found it' means it appeared to him, just as English speakers say 'sunset' without meaning the sun moves. He simply reached the westernmost point of his journey, a shoreline where the sun appeared to sink into dark water. That is phenomenological language, not cosmology. The Abu Dawud hadith's wording is disputed, since some hold the 'spring' phrase belongs to the narrator and not the Prophet, so it cannot establish doctrine. The authentic description, they add, is that the sun 'prostrates beneath the Throne' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3199) — a metaphysical statement rather than a physical one.
sun-muddy-spring.rationale: The Arabic can grammatically bear a phenomenological reading, and the supporting hadith's import is disputed, so this is not admitted. But the phenomenological defence is anachronistic. The parallel rising-place at 18:90, the mirrored structure of the journey, and the earliest tafsir record all show that the first Muslim generations read it as real cosmology, consistent with late-antique Near Eastern belief. The defence requires the earliest interpreters to have misread their own book.

reproductive-science-galen.claim: Quran 86:5-7 says man is created from 'a gushing fluid, proceeding from between the backbone and the ribs'. Semen is produced in the testes, not the torso. The verse echoes the Greek view that semen descends from the region of the back, and classical tafsir took it anatomically. Separately, Quran 23:14 gives the embryonic sequence: drop, then clinging clot, then chewed lump, then bones, then bones clothed with flesh. That tracks Galen's four stages, including Galen's error — bone forming first and then being clothed with flesh, whereas muscle and bone develop concurrently. Medieval Arabic medicine itself mapped the Quranic terms onto Galen's stages. And the embryo is never a 'clot of blood'.
reproductive-science-galen.response: IslamQA 118879, Maurice Bucaille and the iERA embryology paper answer both passages. On 86:5-7, sulb and tara'ib may be a merism for the whole torso, or may refer to the man's loins and the woman's chest, meaning the fluid of both parents. Some modern writers argue the terms denote the embryological origin-sites of the gonads, which do form near the kidneys before descending. On 23:14, the stages are broad visual descriptions accessible to a 7th-century audience. Alaqah means 'clinging thing', which is accurate for implantation, and 'then' need not be strictly sequential. Keith Moore endorsed the compatibility of these terms with modern embryology.
reproductive-science-galen.rationale: The reinterpretations are post hoc. Classical exegetes read 86:7 anatomically, and no reading rescues fluid physically gushing from between backbone and ribs. On embryology, the sequence matches Galen down to sharing Galen's specific bones-then-flesh error, and Muslim physicians for centuries used the Quranic terms as translations of Galen's stages. Keith Moore's endorsement came in a Saudi-sponsored context and is not accepted by the scientific community, and the iERA paper was withdrawn and revised after criticism. A 'broad visual description' that reproduces the precise erroneous schema of the era's dominant Greek medicine is evidence of human sourcing.

mary-sister-of-aaron.claim: The Quran calls Mary the mother of Jesus 'sister of Aaron' (19:28), calls her mother 'the wife of Imran' (3:35), and calls Mary 'daughter of Imran' (66:12). That is exactly the family of Miriam in the Bible: Miriam, daughter of Amram, which is Imran, and sister of Aaron and Moses (Exodus 15:20; Numbers 26:59). She lived about 1,400 years before Mary. The triple match — father Imran, brother Aaron, and the identical name Maryam and Miriam — indicates the two women were conflated. Crucially, this objection is as old as Islam. In Sahih Muslim 2135, the Christians of Najran put precisely this problem to Mughira ibn Shu'ba, and Muhammad's answer was that people 'used to give names after the names of Apostles and pious persons before them'.
mary-sister-of-aaron.response: The Prophet himself answered this in Sahih Muslim 2135, and Abu Amina Elias develops the answer. Semitic naming convention attached people to revered ancestors. 'Sister of Aaron' means a woman of the Aaronic or priestly line — compare Luke 1:5, which calls Elizabeth one 'of the daughters of Aaron', and Mary was her kinswoman. 'Daughter of Imran' likewise denotes descent from the house of Imran, or Amram, and Surah 3 is named 'the Family of Imran', which signals lineage language. So there is no confusion here, only idiom.
mary-sister-of-aaron.rationale: The steelman is real, since Luke 1:5 shows that tribal-descent idiom exists. But it does not cover the evidence. The Quran never uses 'sister of X' as a lineage idiom anywhere else. It does not merely link Mary to Aaron; it gives her the full Exodus family — father Imran, brother Aaron, and the identical name. And 3:35-36 narrates Imran's wife giving birth to Mary as one continuous story. A lineage idiom explains one datum, not three converging ones. That the difficulty was spotted by 7th-century Christians, and required a recorded answer, confirms that the natural reading was and is the problem.

samaritan-anachronism.claim: Quran 20:85-97 says the golden calf at Sinai was made not by Aaron, as in Exodus 32, but by 'al-Samiri' — the Samaritan. The Samaritans as a people emerged after the Assyrian conquest of the northern kingdom, from 722 BC at the earliest, roughly seven centuries after the Exodus period. Scholars note the story likely reflects later anti-Samaritan polemic, since Samaritans were associated with calf-worship at Bethel and Dan, retrojected into the Exodus narrative. The Quran also transfers blame away from Aaron, whom the Bible explicitly names as the calf's maker.
samaritan-anachronism.response: Islamic Awareness argues that 'al-Samiri' is an attributive name for one individual, not necessarily 'the Samaritan'. It could derive from a clan or place name; 1 Kings 16:24 shows 'Shemer' as a personal name predating the city of Samaria. Alternatively, Samaritan tradition itself claims pre-exilic Israelite origins, so the name's referent may be older than critics allow. And the Quran corrects rather than copies the biblical account, by clearing a prophet, Aaron, of idol-making.
samaritan-anachronism.rationale: The etymological escape route is linguistically possible. 'Al-Samiri' need not be an ethnonym, and 'Shemer' as a name is attested early. But it is special pleading against the most natural Arabic reading, in which al-Samiri is exactly the ethnic term as classical usage renders it, and the narrative fits known post-biblical polemical motifs. Neither side can strictly prove the referent, though the critic's reading is the more probable one. And the exoneration of Aaron against Exodus 32 remains a separate, unanswered divergence.

dhul-qarnayn-alexander.claim: The Quran tells of Dhul-Qarnayn, the Two-Horned One. He journeys to the setting-place and the rising-place of the sun. He builds a wall of iron and brass that imprisons Gog and Magog until the end times. That story closely parallels the Syriac Alexander Legend. It is a Christian propaganda text. Its final form dates to about 629-630 AD, with a 6th-century core. Kevin van Bladel published on this in 2008. Tommaso Tesei followed in 2023, with Oxford University Press. Both argue that the Quranic account depends on the legend. The sequence is the same. So is the two-horned motif, since Alexander is horned on his coins. So is the fetid water at the sunset place, and so is the wall. A Greek pagan king, remembered through Christian legend, appears in the Quran as a monotheist hero. And the geography belongs to legend, not to history.
dhul-qarnayn-alexander.response: Three lines are offered in reply. On identity, Maududi and others hold that Dhul-Qarnayn is not Alexander but Cyrus the Great. Cyrus was friendly to monotheists, and he is the two-horned ram of Daniel 8:20. Others say he is an unknown ancient king. On chronology, the Syriac Legend reached its final form about 629-630 AD. That may be too late to be a source for a Meccan surah. So both may draw on a common older oral tradition. On theology, the Quran retells a story its audience already knew. The questions came through Jews, and the Quran corrects the story toward monotheism. A shared narrative frame is not an error. And the Quran omits the legend's explicitly Christian elements.
dhul-qarnayn-alexander.rationale: In academic scholarship the dependence thesis, or at minimum shared legend-matter, is the mainstream view. Tesei dates the core of the legend to the mid-6th century, which dissolves the chronology objection. The Cyrus identification is a 20th-century apologetic with no early tafsir support. Classical exegetes themselves commonly identified Dhul-Qarnayn with Alexander. Even the common-source concession still grants the decisive point. The Quran presents legendary material as factual history — a literal setting-place of the sun, and an eschatological wall no one has found.

cosmology-stars-missiles.claim: The Quran describes the sky as a solid structure: a ceiling held up without visible pillars (13:2; 31:10), which could fall on people in pieces (34:9), with seven stacked heavens (67:3). The lowest is adorned with 'lamps', that is stars, which Allah made 'missiles against the devils' (67:5; compare 37:6-10). Quran 72:8-9 has jinn who ascend to eavesdrop pelted with burning flames. This treats stars and meteors as the same class of object. Meteors are dust grains burning in the atmosphere; stars are distant suns. Mainstream tafsir confirms the reading. Qatada, quoted in Ibn Kathir on 67:5, says: 'These stars were only created for three purposes: adornment for the heaven, missiles for the devils, and signs for navigation.'
cosmology-stars-missiles.response: Ibn Kathir on 67:5, and IslamQA treatments, answer that in Arabic najm and kawkab can denote any luminous heavenly body, including meteors. So 67:5 speaks of luminous projectiles from the lower heaven, not literal suns being thrown. Ibn Kathir himself explains that 'a meteor of fire detaches itself from the star', with the star remaining in place. The seven heavens are unseen metaphysical realms, not physical shells, and canopy language is protective metaphor, since the atmosphere genuinely does shield the earth. These verses describe the unseen, which is a theological datum and not falsifiable by astronomy.
cosmology-stars-missiles.rationale: Quran 67:5 identifies the objects made into missiles as the same 'lamps' that adorn the lowest heaven, which are the visible stars, and Qatada's mainstream tafsir states exactly that. Ibn Kathir's detaching-meteor gloss is itself an attempted harmonisation, and it still ties meteors physically to stars, which is false. The reading fits precisely the 7th-century phenomenology of shooting stars. The metaphysical-realms defence is viable in isolation, but the missile verses anchor the cosmology to visible objects.

abrogation-satanic-verses.claim: Quran 2:106 and 16:101 state that Allah replaces some revealed verses with others. Critics ask why an omniscient God's eternal speech needs cancelling and reissuing within 23 years, and 16:101 records that contemporaries concluded 'You are but a forger.' The sharpest test case is the satanic-verses incident. Early Islamic sources — al-Tabari, Ibn Sa'd and al-Waqidi — record that Muhammad, wishing for reconciliation with the Quraysh, recited praise of the goddesses al-Lat, al-Uzza and Manat after 53:19-20: 'these are the exalted cranes whose intercession is hoped for'. The words were later attributed to Satan and cancelled. Early exegetes read 22:52 — 'Satan threw something into the recitation of every prophet' — as the divine comment on the event. Shahab Ahmed of Harvard, in 'Before Orthodoxy', showed that the incident was a standard element of Muslim historical memory for Islam's first 150 years or so, and only later became universally rejected.
abrogation-satanic-verses.response: On abrogation, SeekersGuidance answers that naskh is progressive legislation, not divine self-correction. It is staged pedagogy — alcohol was banned in three steps — and each ruling was perfect for its time. Jewish and Christian scripture also supersedes earlier law, in the sacrificial system and in Acts 10. On the satanic verses, al-Albani in 'Nasb al-Majaniq' and others answer on the chains. Every chain of the story is broken, with no Companion eyewitness. It is absent from Bukhari and Muslim. It contradicts the Quran's own guarantee at 53:3-4. And its many mutually contradictory versions mark it as storyteller material. Scholars from Ibn Khuzaymah, who called it 'a fabrication of the heretics', to al-Albani have rejected it on transmission grounds.
abrogation-satanic-verses.rationale: Two components, two results. Abrogation as a phenomenon is conceded, since 2:106 is explicit and classical scholarship catalogued abrogated verses. Whether it is a defect is a theological judgment, and the progressive-legislation steelman is coherent. On the satanic-verses incident, Shahab Ahmed's demonstration of early universal acceptance is historically weighty, and 22:52 with 17:73-75 read most naturally as responses to a real event. But the chain criticism is genuine, since no single sound chain exists, so on this app's own evidence standard it cannot be graded admitted. The historical-critical case is stronger than most Muslims allow, and the chain case is stronger than most critics allow.

compilation-lost-verses.claim: Against the perfect-preservation claim of 15:9, the Sahih sources record five things. Sahih al-Bukhari 4986 says no compiled Quran existed at Muhammad's death; after heavy reciter casualties at Yamama, Umar feared 'a large part of the Quran may be lost', and Zayd ibn Thabit collected it 'from palm-leaf stalks, thin white stones, and the hearts of men', with the ending of Surah at-Tawbah found with only one man. Sahih Muslim 1452a has Aisha state that the 'five sucklings' wording 'was recited as part of the Quran' when the Prophet died, yet it is in no mushaf. Umar in Sahih al-Bukhari 6829 affirms the stoning verse was revealed and recited; it too is absent. Sunan Ibn Majah 1944 has Aisha say the page with those verses was under her bedding and 'a tame sheep came in and ate it' — the report is graded hasan, though the sheep detail rides on a weak chain, and the loss it narrates is independently attested in Sahih Muslim. And Abu Musa in Sahih Muslim 1050 says: 'we used to recite a surah resembling Bara'ah... I have forgotten it.'
compilation-lost-verses.response: Al-Azami, IslamQA 175355 and ICRAA answer that preservation was primarily oral. Hundreds of memorisers carried the complete text, so Zayd's written collection was a verification exercise over an already-memorised whole; 'found with only one man' means only one written copy, not only one memory. The 'missing' verses fall under divinely intended abrogation of recitation, naskh al-tilawah. The stoning and suckling wordings had their recitation withdrawn while, for stoning, the ruling remained, and 2:106 explicitly includes verses 'caused to be forgotten'. The sheep story is weak and is contradicted by stronger chains without it. Al-Azami's monograph argues the compilation methodology was the most rigorous in the history of any scripture.
compilation-lost-verses.rationale: The load-bearing facts are all in Sahih collections and are conceded by mainstream scholarship: no complete compiled codex at the Prophet's death, fear of loss at Yamama, wordings believed by Companions to be Quran that are not in today's Quran, and a whole forgotten surah reported. The naskh al-tilawah defence is the concession dressed in doctrine. It grants that recited Quranic material exited the text and explains it as intentional. That is unfalsifiable and circular. Any lost verse can be declared abrogated in recitation after the fact, on the authority of the very reports that show the loss. The guarantee of 15:9 is maintained only by definitional manoeuvre.

uthman-standardization-qiraat.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 records that during Uthman's reign Muslims 'differed in their recitation' so sharply that Hudhayfa feared division 'as Jews and Christians differed'. Uthman had one recension copied and 'ordered that all the other Quranic materials, whether fragmentary manuscripts or whole copies, be burnt'. Companion codices were suppressed. Ibn Mas'ud's reportedly lacked Surahs 1, 113 and 114; Ubayy's contained two extra. Aisha and Hafsa both had 2:238 with the added words 'and the asr prayer' (Sahih Muslim 629; Sahih al-Bukhari 5005). Today the Quran is printed in materially different reading traditions. Hafs is used by most of the world, and Warsh across North and West Africa; they differ in hundreds of places, some of them semantic, such as 3:146. The Sanaa palimpsest's lower text shows a pre-Uthmanic text-form, and Daniel Brubaker has documented thousands of physical corrections in early manuscripts. A single letter-perfect text transmitted unchanged is not what the record shows.
uthman-standardization-qiraat.response: Al-Azami, Islamic Awareness and the IRCICA reply by Altikulac answer as follows. The Quran was revealed in seven ahruf, or modes, all divinely revealed. Uthman's standardisation eliminated no revelation; it unified the community on one mode to prevent schism, with the Companions' unanimous approval. The canonical readings, Hafs and Warsh among them, are parallel mass-transmitted recitations going back to the Prophet. They are dialect and permitted variation, not corruption, and virtually none affect doctrine. Companion codices were personal copies with explanatory notes, not rival Qurans. Brubaker's corrections are routine scribal fixes toward the standard text, which is a sign of careful control. And radiocarbon-dated early manuscripts, at Birmingham and Tübingen, match today's text extraordinarily closely. No other ancient book is this stable.
uthman-standardization-qiraat.rationale: The facts are not in dispute. There was a mass burning of variant codices by state order. Companion codices differed in wording, and in surah count per early sources. Wives of the Prophet attested different wording for 2:238. And two materially different texts are printed today. All of that comes from Sahih hadith, from classical qira'at literature, and from print editions anyone can buy. What is contested is only the interpretation: divinely sanctioned modes, or suppressed plurality. Fairness requires noting the steelman's genuine strength, since early Qurans after Uthman are remarkably stable. But 'perfect preservation of one exact text' is refuted by Islam's own canon. What was preserved is the Uthmanic recension, achieved by destroying the evidence of what else existed.

aisha-age.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 5134, also at 3894, and Sahih Muslim 1422 record it from Aisha herself. The Prophet married her when she was six. He consummated the marriage when she was nine. Sahih al-Bukhari 6130 adds that she was playing with dolls at his house. These are among the most multiply attested facts in the hadith corpus. They were accepted by all classical scholars, and nine-year consummation became a benchmark in law. The issue binds Islam for two reasons. Muhammad is the 'excellent pattern' for all time (33:21). And 65:4 gives a divorce waiting-period for wives 'who have not yet menstruated', which classical tafsir applies to marriage before puberty.
aisha-age.response: Two incompatible defences circulate. The revisionist one holds that Aisha was really about 15 to 19, arguing from her sister Asma's reported age and other inferences. The traditional-contextualist one is the scholarly mainstream, set out by Jonathan A. C. Brown in his Yaqeen Institute paper. On that view the ages are authentic and revisionism is bad hadith methodology. Instead the marriage must be judged in context. Betrothal of minors, with consummation at puberty, was normal across premodern societies. That included the Jewish and Christian law of the era. No contemporary or enemy of Muhammad ever criticised it. Aisha reports it without complaint and became Islam's greatest female scholar. And the marriage was commanded in a dream-revelation.
aisha-age.rationale: The ages are conceded in the strongest possible Islamic sources — Aisha's own first-person narration in both Bukhari and Muslim, through multiple chains. The flagship traditionalist institution explicitly rejects the revisionist escape as methodologically indefensible, since no classical scholar in 1,300 years doubted the ages. So the live debate is only over the moral evaluation. That is a genuine argument, and it concedes every fact. For fairness, say plainly that such marriages were unremarkable in antiquity. The Christian critique properly targets the claim that this man is the timeless moral exemplar (33:21). It does not target 7th-century norms as such.

women-and-captives.claim: Quran 4:34 instructs that wives whose rebellion is feared be admonished, then abandoned in bed, then struck. The verb is daraba, rendered 'beat' or 'strike' by the overwhelming majority of translators, and classical tafsir universally understood physical hitting, qualified as not severe. Sunan Abi Dawud 2146 records the trajectory: 'Do not beat Allah's handmaidens', then permission after Umar's complaint, then, when women complained, 'those men are not the best of you'. Separately, 4:24 permits intercourse with married captive women, their prior marriages annulled by capture. Sahih Muslim 1438 shows companions on the Banu Mustaliq raid asking about coitus interruptus with newly captured women, where the objection recorded concerns the futility of thwarting what is decreed, not the act itself.
women-and-captives.response: IslamQA 20802, classical fiqh and Jonathan Brown's Slavery and Islam answer as follows. On 4:34, the permission is a last resort and symbolic. Classical jurisprudence forbade injury, bruising, or striking the face. The Prophet never hit a wife or servant (Sahih Muslim 2328) and said 'the best of you are best to their wives'. Some modern scholars read daraba as 'separate from', and Ayesha Chaudhry's Oxford study traces the whole debate. The three steps are de-escalation in a context where unrestricted beating was normal, so the verse restricts violence rather than licensing it. On captives, concubinage was the universal law of war in antiquity, including in biblical law (Numbers 31:18; Deuteronomy 21:10-14). Islam regulated it with a waiting period before intercourse, forbade splitting captives from their children, and praised freeing and marrying a captive. It channelled captives into households rather than massacre, on a trajectory toward abolition.
women-and-captives.rationale: Both permissions are conceded textually and juristically. No classical authority denied that 4:34 authorises some physical striking; the dispute is over degree. Sexual access to captives is affirmed by the context of 4:24, by Sahih Muslim 1438, and by mainstream fatwa — IslamQA states it plainly today. The restriction-trajectory steelman is historically serious, and the comparison with Deuteronomy 21 must be honestly faced rather than dodged. But the Christian critique lands on the exemplar claim. These are presented not as regulated concessions of a hard era, but as the final revelation's permanent legislation, and they are defended as such by living mainstream authorities. The 'daraba means separate' reading is rejected by essentially all classical and most contemporary scholarship.

zaynab-hastening-revelation.claim: Quran 33:37 addresses Muhammad's marriage to Zaynab bint Jahsh, the former wife of his adopted son Zayd — a scandal under Arab adoption norms. The verse reveals that while Muhammad concealed his interest and feared people's talk, Allah married her to him 'so that there would be no blame on believers concerning the wives of their adopted sons'. The Quran simultaneously abolished adoption's legal force (33:4-5). Critics observe a recurring pattern of revelations authorising Muhammad's personal privileges: unlimited wives for him alone (33:50), freedom to reschedule his wives' turns (33:51), and a ban on other men marrying his widows (33:53). The pattern was visible in his own house. After 33:51 came down, Aisha said to him: 'I feel that your Lord hastens in fulfilling your wishes and desires' (Sahih al-Bukhari 4788).
zaynab-hastening-revelation.response: ICRAA, Ibn Kathir and Maududi answer that the marriage was a costly legal reform, not indulgence. Pre-Islamic adoption created fictive bloodlines with real inheritance and marriage consequences. Abolishing it required a public, unavoidable demonstration, and God chose the hardest case, the Prophet himself, because no one else's example would have broken the taboo. Muhammad resisted — 'you feared the people' — which is evidence against opportunism. Zaynab was his cousin, whom he could have married years earlier had desire driven him. Aisha's remark was spousal candour, and that Muslims faithfully preserved even this barb in their most authentic collection shows the tradition's honesty. His marriages overall skewed toward widows and political alliances.
zaynab-hastening-revelation.rationale: Every factual element is canonical. The desire-then-revelation sequence is in the Quran's own wording. The privileges of 33:50-53 are explicit. And the 'hastens to fulfil your desires' observation is Aisha's, in Bukhari. The legal-reform steelman is internally coherent for Zaynab taken alone, but it cannot explain the cumulative pattern. The 'preserved barb proves honesty' argument also cuts both ways. It proves the tradition is honest, and that what it honestly preserves is contemporaneous suspicion inside the Prophet's own house. Whether the pattern proves fabrication is a judgment call. That the pattern exists is admitted in Islam's canon.

prophet-test-signs.claim: The biblical test of a prophet is verifiable prediction (Deuteronomy 18:21-22; Isaiah 41:21-23) and God-given signs (John 10:37-38). The Quran repeatedly records Muhammad declining to produce signs: 'Why has a sign not been sent down to him? Say: signs are only with Allah, and I am only a clear warner' (29:50; also 13:7; 17:90-93; 6:37). Public miracles appear only in later hadith, which sits in tension with the Quran's own stance. The one claimed predictive prophecy is 30:2-4: 'The Romans have been defeated... but they will be victorious within three to nine years.' It is problematic on three counts. In the original undotted script the words could equally be read 'Rome has conquered... will be defeated'. The timespan is elastic. And on standard dating, from Jerusalem in 614 to final victory in 628, fulfilment falls outside nine years. A vague geopolitical reversal cannot meet Deuteronomy 18's standard of detailed, falsifiable prediction.
prophet-test-signs.response: About Islam and Ibn Kathir answer on both points. The Rome prophecy was made when Byzantium lay prostrate, so predicting its victory was humanly absurd — and it happened, since Heraclius' improbable campaigns between 622 and 628 reversed the war. Abu Bakr's public wager (Jami at-Tirmidhi 3194) shows that 'Rome will win' was the reading from the start, and the recitation consensus fixes it. The same passage adds that the believers would rejoice at the same time, which was fulfilled at Badr. On signs, the Quran denies signs on demand to hostile testers, not miracles absolutely. The Quran's own inimitability, in the unanswered challenge of 2:23, is the standing miracle, and the splitting of the moon is referenced in 54:1-2 itself.
prophet-test-signs.rationale: The Rome passage is a genuine pre-event prediction by any dating, so 'no prophecy at all' overstates the case, and Abu Bakr's wager is early evidence for the standard reading. But it survives as prophecy only in its vaguest form. The counter-reading in the defective script is real. The three-to-nine-year window fits only with favourable date choices. And one elastic reversal cannot bear the weight Deuteronomy 18 places on detailed, falsifiable prediction. Compare Isaiah naming Cyrus. The signs question is likewise split. The Quran's own posture, a warner without signs, is textually clear. It stands in real tension with the later hadith miracle corpus, which multiplies wonders the Quran never claims.

aorta-test.claim: Quran 69:44-46 says: 'If he had invented false sayings concerning Us, We would have seized him by the right hand, then We would have cut from him the aorta.' In Sahih al-Bukhari 4428, during his fatal illness, Muhammad says: 'O Aisha! I still feel the pain caused by the food I ate at Khaybar, and at this time I feel as if my aorta is being cut from that poison.' The poisoned meat was served by a Jewish woman after Khaybar's conquest, reportedly to test his prophethood, since she reasoned that a true prophet would be informed. The internal-test argument runs like this. The Quran names a specific divine punishment for a false prophet, a severed aorta. Islam's most authentic source records Muhammad dying while describing exactly that sensation, from a poisoning administered as a test of prophethood. His companion Bishr died of the same meal.
aorta-test.response: IslamQA and Islamweb answer on the text. Quran 69:44-46 describes an immediate, public divine execution for forgery — seizure 'by the right hand' and instant severing, as a demonstration. It does not describe death by illness more than three years after a poisoning, since Khaybar was in 628 and the death in 632. 'I feel as if my aorta is being cut' is an Arabic idiom for mortal agony, using a different anatomical word — abhar rather than watin — so it is a simile of pain, not a report of the punishment in 69:46. Far from disproving him, the episode is claimed as vindication. The meat itself 'spoke' to warn him, he stopped eating, and death from its lingering effect earned him a martyr's honour, after the religion was completed (5:3). No forger controls his dying words, and attributing his death to the poison shows guileless candour.
aorta-test.rationale: The factual chain is fully canonical. The verse, the poisoning as a test of prophethood, and the deathbed aorta statement are all in Bukhari. But the argument's force depends on reading 69:44-46 as a general criterion rather than as a threat of immediate exemplary execution. The Arabic uses different anatomical terms, and 'as if' marks a simile. The Christian can fairly say it is at minimum an astonishing irony that Islam's own canon has its prophet dying while describing the false prophet's punishment, poisoned in a test whose stated logic the outcome appeared to vindicate. The Muslim can fairly say the verse does not state the general criterion the argument needs. Powerful rhetoric; not a strict internal contradiction.

salvation-scales.claim: Islamic salvation is a weighing: 'Those whose scales are heavy — they are the successful; those whose scales are light — they have lost their souls, in Hell abiding' (23:102-103; 101:6-9; 7:8-9). Allah's love is conditional: 'Allah loves not the disbelievers' (3:32). Assurance is absent by design, even for Muhammad. 'By Allah, though I am Allah's Messenger, I neither know what will happen to me, nor to you' (Sahih al-Bukhari 7018, echoing Quran 46:9). And: 'none of you will enter Paradise by his deeds... not even I, unless Allah covers me with mercy' (Sahih Muslim 2816). The contrast is structural. The God of the Bible demonstrates love for sinners while they are still sinners (Romans 5:8). Salvation is by grace through faith and not by works (Ephesians 2:8-9). Sins are borne by a substitute (Isaiah 53:5-6). And assurance is offered as knowledge: 'that you may know that you have eternal life' (1 John 5:13).
salvation-scales.response: The Yaqeen Institute's papers on salvation, and Ibn Qayyim on fear and hope, answer that Islam's soteriology is saturated with mercy rather than cold bookkeeping. Allah's mercy 'prevails over His wrath'. One good deed counts tenfold to seven-hundredfold, while a sin counts once (Sahih al-Bukhari 6491). Sincere monotheism ultimately delivers from eternal Hell, and Sahih Muslim 2816 shows that entry to Paradise is itself by Allah's mercy and not earned — which is functionally a doctrine of grace. The absence of presumptuous assurance is a feature, holding the believer between fear and hope, producing humility and moral seriousness, whereas guaranteed salvation invites licence; Christians themselves debate eternal security. Quran 3:32 concerns Allah's love of approval for persistent rejecters, not the absence of universal compassion (7:156). And Bukhari 7018 predates the revelation of Muhammad's forgiveness (48:1-2).
salvation-scales.rationale: This entry documents a structural contrast, and every element of the Islamic side is canonical and conceded: salvation weighed by scales, no textual offer of assurance, conditional divine love in the Quran's explicit wording, and Muhammad's own recorded uncertainty. Note that 48:1-2 rescues Muhammad specifically, which underlines that others lack the guarantee. The steelman honestly complicates the caricature, since Muslim 2816 does place final entry on mercy. But mercy applied through a merit-weighing frame, with no substitutionary atonement and no offered assurance, remains categorically different from Romans 5:8 and 1 John 5:13. This is the entry that leads most directly to the gospel.

taqiyya-deception.claim: Islamic sources do allow deceit in set cases. Quran 16:106 excuses one who denies the faith under force. Quran 3:28 allows one to hide it from hostile unbelievers. The word there is tuqah, the root of taqiyya, which grew mainly in Shia law under attack. Sunni sources allow lying in three cases: war, making peace between people, and between spouses. That list is in Sahih Muslim 2605, where it comes through the narrator Ibn Shihab, and in Jami at-Tirmidhi 1939. Muhammad said 'war is deceit' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3030). He also allowed false speech in the killing of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf (Sahih al-Bukhari 3031). Scripture runs the other way: God 'cannot lie' (Titus 1:2), and truth under threat is the martyr's calling (Matthew 10:28; Revelation 2:10). But the loud claim, that Muslims are told to lie to us about their faith, goes far beyond the sources. Hiding faith under threat is not a general licence, and Sunni teaching treats lying as a grave sin outside those cases.
taqiyya-deception.response: IslamQA 27261 replies that this is a narrow rule for survival, not a way of life. It is much like Peter's denial being forgiven. The three cases cover the sort of peace-making many would accept. 'War is deceit' describes battle craft, which every army uses. And the base rule is truth: 'truthfulness leads to righteousness' (Sahih al-Bukhari 6094). False witness is among the worst sins. The idea that Muslims lie to non-Muslims as a habit is, they note, a stereotype that no mainstream ruling supports.
taqiyya-deception.rationale: Both halves of this entry matter. The facts are real. Deceit is allowed in set cases — war, force, peace-making, spouses — in sahih sources, and that differs from the call to truth unto death. But the loud claim, that you cannot trust a word a Muslim says, has no basis in Islamic law and poisons every talk. The rule is simple. Know the doctrine. Never aim it at the person in front of you. To accuse an ordinary Sunni of it is unfair, unprovable, and ends the conversation on the spot.

sharia-apostasy-jizya.claim: Classical Islamic law prescribes death for leaving Islam: 'Whoever changes his religion, kill him' (Sahih al-Bukhari 6922; compare 6878, which lists apostasy among the three grounds for lawful killing). All four Sunni schools carried the ruling, and it remains law in several states today. Quran 9:29 commands fighting the People of the Book 'until they pay the jizya willingly while they are humbled', establishing the dhimmi system of subordinated tolerance. Hudud punishments include amputation for theft (5:38) and stoning for adultery, from the sunnah (Sahih al-Bukhari 6829; Sahih Muslim 1690). The New Testament contrast is sharp.
