Faith is uncoerced — 'If anyone hears my words and does not keep them, I do not judge him' (John 12:47) — and the wheat and tares grow together till harvest (Matthew 13:29-30). The sword is renounced for the gospel's spread (Matthew 26:52; John 18:36). And apostates are to be won back, not executed (2 Timothy 2:24-26).
sharia-apostasy-jizya.response: Reform-minded Muslim scholars argue from inside the tradition. 'No compulsion in religion' (2:256) is the Quran's own principle, and the Quran itself prescribes no worldly penalty for apostasy. The death penalty rests on hadith, and is best understood historically as punishing treason against the Muslim polity in wartime rather than private belief change — a view advanced by scholars such as Jonathan Brown and Taha Jabir Alalwani, and adopted by some modern states. Jizya was a tax in lieu of military service, often lighter than the zakat Muslims paid, and dhimmi status provided real protection that was unusual for its era. Hudud punishments carry near-impossible evidentiary standards, such as four eyewitnesses to the act, designed to make application rare — deterrence theatre more than practice.
sharia-apostasy-jizya.rationale: The provisions themselves are admitted. The apostasy hadith is in Bukhari, all four classical schools carried the ruling, mainstream fatwa sites still affirm it, and roughly a dozen states criminalise apostasy today, several of them capitally. The reformist steelman is genuine scholarship, but it argues against the classical consensus rather than against the sources' existence, and 'no compulsion' must be harmonised by every reformer precisely because the coercive texts are there. The practical stake for evangelism is pastoral, not polemical. This is why your Muslim friend's hesitation is not stubbornness. It is why security and confidentiality for seekers are non-negotiable. And it is why counting the cost (Luke 14:28) is part of sharing the gospel with Muslims.

allah-moon-god.claim: A popular claim in Christian counter-apologetics, popularised by Robert Morey's 'The Moon-God Allah' in 1994, holds that Allah was originally a pagan Arabian moon deity. It is often linked to the crescent symbol and to the South Arabian god Sin, or to Hubal. The conclusion drawn is that Muslims worship a repackaged idol. The argument circulates widely in tracts and online despite its evidentiary problems.
allah-moon-god.response: The rebuttal here is not a Muslim response but the evidence itself, acknowledged across the scholarly spectrum, including by Christian missiologists. 'Allah' is the ordinary Arabic word for God — the cognate of Hebrew Elohim and Aramaic Alaha. It was used by Arabic-speaking Jews and Christians before Islam, and it appears in every Arabic Bible to this day; Genesis 1:1 in Arabic begins 'In the beginning Allah created'. The Quran explicitly condemns worship of the moon: 'Do not prostrate to the sun or the moon' (41:37). The crescent symbol entered Islamic use centuries later, through the Ottomans. And Morey's archaeological linkages, including Hubal and the Sin temple at Hazor, are rejected by the relevant specialists.
allah-moon-god.rationale: Fairly weighed, this criticism fails. The linguistic evidence defeats the thesis — Allah is the standard Semitic word for God, used by pre-Islamic Christians and in Arabic Bibles today — as does the Quran's own prohibition of moon-worship. Rick Brown published the refutation in the International Journal of Frontier Missions in 2006, so Christian scholars of missions have themselves done this work. The real dispute with Islam is about God's character and triunity, not about the Arabic word for him. Christians who use the moon-god argument hand every informed Muslim an easy win and discredit their stronger arguments. It is marked answered so that you never make this mistake.

quran-late-composition.claim: In the 1970s some scholars argued that the Quran took shape long after Muhammad. John Wansbrough made the case. Patricia Crone and Michael Cook made a like case in 'Hagarism'. On that view the text was pieced together from shared lore across the Near East, one or two centuries later. It is still repeated in some sceptical and Christian writing as if it were settled.
quran-late-composition.response: The evidence answered the theory. Carbon dating puts the Birmingham Quran leaf at 568 to 645 AD, with 95.4% confidence. That test dates the animal skin, not the ink. The range falls in or just after the life of Muhammad. The lower text of the Sanaa leaves is 7th century too. Behnam Sadeghi and Mohsen Goudarzi wrote on Sanaa in 2012. Nicolai Sinai asked in 2014 when the bare consonant text was closed. Scholars now hold that it was largely fixed by the middle of the 7th century. That includes Sinai, Sadeghi, and even those friendly to the revisionists. The late-date thesis is dead in the field.
quran-late-composition.rationale: Weighed fairly, this claim fails. The old copies date the text to the 7th century, and serious scholars across the field accept an early consonant text. Note what that does not give away. Early is not the same as kept whole. The Uthman case and the lost-verses case still stand, and both sit in Bukhari. Early is not the same as true, either. But a Christian who says the Quran was made up centuries later is fighting the evidence. He is also cutting his own rope, since the same tests support how the Bible came down to us. It is marked answered to keep the strong arguments clean.

spread-only-by-sword.claim: A common line holds that Islam grew by force alone. On that account, people were made to convert wherever Muslim armies won. The claim is then set against the early church, which grew while under attack.
spread-only-by-sword.response: The record answers the caricature. The armies did conquer fast. But conversion was slow, and mostly by choice. Richard Bulliet studied conversion curves. He found that Egypt, Syria and Persia stayed mostly non-Muslim for two to three centuries under Muslim rule. Ira Lapidus records the same pattern. The reason lies in the tax. The jizya and dhimmi system assumed large non-Muslim populations, and you cannot tax converts you have forced. Indonesia is the largest Muslim country on earth, and no Arab army ever took it. Islam arrived there through traders and Sufi networks, as it did in much of West Africa. Forced conversions did happen, but they were rare, and jurists often condemned them citing 2:256, 'no compulsion in religion'.
spread-only-by-sword.rationale: Weighed fairly, the 'only by the sword' claim fails. Conquest and conversion were two different things, and the tax system proves it. What survives is the narrower point made elsewhere on this site. Islamic law does contain coercive rules, including death for apostasy and jizya paid 'while they are humbled'. The New Testament has no parallel to those. And the order Islam built favoured conversion in one direction only. Argue that documented gap, not the caricature. It is marked answered so the credible version of the argument stays credible.

inheritance-math-awl.claim: Quran 4:11-12 and 4:176 assign fixed inheritance fractions, and in common cases they add up to more than the estate. A man leaving a wife, two daughters and both parents yields one eighth plus two thirds plus one third, which is 27/24. A man leaving a mother, a wife and two sisters yields one third plus one quarter plus two thirds, which is 15/12. Islamic jurisprudence itself acknowledges the oversubscription. The doctrine of awl, a proportional reduction of all shares, was devised to handle it. By IslamQA's own account, no case of awl arose under Muhammad or Abu Bakr; the caliph Umar was the first to rule on it. So the Quran's 'perfectly detailed' law (6:114) required a human patch within a decade of Muhammad's death. A book claiming divine authorship and precision in its most legally binding passages should not need companions to renormalise its fractions.
inheritance-math-awl.response: Muslim jurists respond that the verses assign shares, not a summed distribution formula. When shares oversubscribe, awl preserves each heir's proportion relative to the others, which they argue is the intended design — a ratio system, not an addition problem. IslamOnline argues that the internal proportions remain exactly as stated even when the denominators are scaled, so no mathematical error exists. IslamQA adds that the companions' consensus on awl demonstrates the system's flexibility rather than a defect, and that the Quran never promises the fractions will sum to one in every configuration.
inheritance-math-awl.rationale: The controlling facts are conceded on the Islamic side. The fractions do exceed the estate in ordinary cases, and awl was a post-Muhammad juristic invention first ruled on by Umar — IslamQA states this plainly. The dispute is only over characterisation, ratios rather than sums. But the verses read as direct commands about actual portions of actual estates, closing with 'an obligation from Allah' (4:11), and the ratio defence is nowhere in the text. It was reverse-engineered after real estates came up short. This is graded admitted rather than unrefuted because the substance — that shares oversubscribe, and that humans patched it — is affirmed by Islamic jurisprudence itself.

banu-qurayza-massacre.claim: In 627 AD, after the Battle of the Trench, the Jewish tribe Banu Qurayza surrendered to Muhammad. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh ruled that 'their warriors be killed and their children taken captive', and Muhammad endorsed the verdict as 'the judgment of Allah' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3043). Ibn Ishaq's sira records 600 to 900 males beheaded in trenches dug in Medina's market, with Muhammad present. The women and children were enslaved, and Muhammad took Rayhana from among the captives. Adulthood was determined by inspecting for pubic hair; the survivor Atiyya al-Qurazi testifies to this directly (Sunan Abi Dawud 4404). These are not enemy accusations. Every detail comes from Islam's own canonical hadith and earliest biography. The evangelistic contrast is stark, since 'by their fruits you will know them' (Matthew 7:15-20) is applied to the man Muslims must take as the perfect model (Quran 33:21).
banu-qurayza-massacre.response: SeekersGuidance answers that Banu Qurayza committed high treason during an existential siege. They broke their defence pact by negotiating with the attacking confederates. The penalty was wartime justice for treachery, not religious persecution. The verdict was delivered by Sa'd, an arbitrator the tribe itself accepted. SeekersGuidance also argues that it matched the tribe's own law in Deuteronomy 20:10-14, for a besieged and treacherous city. Some modern academics, following W. N. Arafat, dispute the 600 to 900 figure as an exaggeration absorbed from Jewish narrators, and argue that only the guilty leaders were executed.
banu-qurayza-massacre.rationale: The event itself is not denied by mainstream Islam; the defences justify it. Bukhari preserves the judgment and Muhammad's endorsement. Abu Dawud preserves the puberty inspections. The sira supplies the scale. The Deuteronomy 20 parallel fails on its own terms, since that law addressed distant cities in Israel's unique theocratic conquest, was never a standing model, and Muhammad claimed a universal, final revelation of mercy (21:107). The Arafat revisionist number is rejected by M. J. Kister's classic study, and it sits awkwardly with the sahih material. What remains conceded on all sides is the mass execution of surrendered prisoners, the enslavement of their families, and the claim that the man who presided is humanity's perfect example.

muhammad-in-the-bible.claim: The Quran stakes its credibility on Muhammad being 'written in the Torah and the Gospel' (7:157), and on Jesus foretelling 'a messenger after me whose name is Ahmad' (61:6). The three standard proof-texts all fail on inspection. Deuteronomy 18:15-18 requires a prophet 'from among your brothers', meaning the Israelites, since Deuteronomy 18:2 uses 'brothers' of fellow tribes. Acts 3:22 identifies him as Jesus. Muhammad was not an Israelite, mediated no covenant, and by Islam's own account performed no confirming signs. The Paraclete of John 14-16 is 'the Spirit of truth', whom 'the world cannot see', who 'will be in you', and whom the disciples themselves would receive — impossible for a man born five centuries later. The periklytos conjecture has no manuscript support. And Song of Songs 5:16's machamaddim is a common noun, plural, meaning 'altogether desirable', used of the Shulamite's beloved, not a name. The dilemma bites both ways: if the Bible was corrupted, why does the Quran send Muslims to it to find Muhammad?
muhammad-in-the-bible.response: Dawah apologists, including Ahmed Deedat, Zakir Naik and Discover The Truth, argue as follows. 'Brothers' of the Israelites means their kin, the Ishmaelites. Muhammad parallels Moses more closely than Jesus does — natural birth, marriage, law-giving, migration, military leadership, and natural death — all points where Jesus, as divine Son, differs. The Paraclete passages were altered, or parakletos is a corruption of an original periklytos, 'the praised one', which is Ahmad. And machamaddim carries the very consonantal root of Muhammad's name, in a messianic love-song. They add that Quran 7:157 is corroborated precisely because traces survive despite centuries of transmission by hostile communities.
muhammad-in-the-bible.rationale: The Christian rebuttal stands essentially unanswered on the textual level. Deuteronomy 18:2 and 17:15 fix 'brothers' as Israelites. Deuteronomy 34:10-12 defines 'like Moses' by signs, wonders, and knowing God face to face — the exact credentials Islam denies Muhammad (Quran 29:50-51). Every Greek manuscript of John reads parakletos, and the periklytos emendation is pure conjecture. Machamaddim is standard Hebrew vocabulary, used also in Song 2:3 and Hosea 9:16. Most decisively, the argument self-destructs. Quran 7:157 presupposes a readable, reliable Torah and Gospel in the 7th century, which feeds directly into this site's central tahrif dilemma. No Muslim response engages that circularity successfully.

ishmael-covenant-kaaba.claim: Islam's foundation story runs through Abraham. The covenant passes through Ishmael, Abraham and Ishmael built the Kaaba in Mecca (Quran 2:127; 3:96), and the near-sacrifice was of Ishmael. Genesis says the opposite. God establishes his everlasting covenant through Isaac, explicitly not Ishmael, though Ishmael is blessed (Genesis 17:19-21; 21:12), and the sacrifice is of 'your son, your only son Isaac' at Moriah (22:2). Strikingly, the Quran never names the sacrificed son (37:100-107), and early Muslim exegesis was split — al-Tabari, Islam's greatest classical commentator, concluded from the Quran's own sequence that it was Isaac. No pre-Islamic source of any kind places Abraham within a thousand miles of Mecca, and Genesis locates Ishmael's line in Paran and Shur, in north-west Arabia and Sinai, not the Hijaz. The Islamic claim requires the Torah to be textually corrupted at exactly these points, which lands in the tahrif trap: the Quran affirms the Torah in Muhammad's hands, and the manuscripts predate him.
ishmael-covenant-kaaba.response: Islamic Awareness and other Muslim apologists argue that the Torah's 'your only son Isaac' betrays later Israelite editing. Ishmael was Abraham's only son for about fourteen years, so 'only son' fits him alone, and a scribe allegedly inserted Isaac's name. They read Genesis 21:21's Paran as extending to the Hijaz. They connect Psalm 84:6's 'valley of Baca' with Bakkah, or Mecca, in Quran 3:96. They take Sahih al-Bukhari 3364's detailed Abraham-in-Mecca narrative as preserved true history. And Islamic Awareness contends that the Quran's silence on the son's name is deliberate universality, while the later consensus for Ishmael rests on sound reasoning from the sequence of events in Surah 37.
ishmael-covenant-kaaba.rationale: Every leg of the Muslim case depends on assuming Genesis corruption without manuscript evidence. The Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint carry Genesis 17 and 22 unchanged from centuries before Christ, let alone before Muhammad. The 'only son' argument concedes the method, which is to rewrite the text to fit the claim. Al-Tabari's verdict for Isaac shows that even Islam's classical scholarship could not read Ishmael out of Surah 37. Paran is fixed near Sinai by Genesis 14:6 and Numbers 10-13, and Baca is a valley on the road to Zion (Psalm 84:7). No pre-Islamic trace of an Abrahamic Kaaba exists. The claim survives only inside the tahrif assumption that this site's core dilemma already dismantles.

quran-borrowed-legends.claim: Several Quranic narratives track post-biblical Jewish and Christian legends rather than the Bible. Quran 5:32 — 'whoever kills a soul... it is as if he killed all mankind' — reproduces Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5, a rabbinic homily on Cain composed centuries before Islam, and it even keeps the Israel-specific framing, 'We decreed upon the Children of Israel'. The preceding verse's raven, who shows Cain how to bury Abel (5:31), parallels the same midrashic cluster. Quran 18:9-26 retells the Seven Sleepers of Ephesus, a Christian legend attested in Jacob of Serugh, who died in 521, and in Gregory of Tours, complete with the dog and the disputed head-count, presented as revelation about real 'youths of the cave'. Quran 21:68-69 has Abraham thrown into a fire, a story that arose from Genesis Rabbah's wordplay, reading 'Ur' of the Chaldees as ur, 'fire'. A book delivering eternal truth should not canonise identifiable human commentary, folklore and a pun as history.
quran-borrowed-legends.response: Islamic Awareness and similar apologists respond on three fronts. A parallel does not prove borrowing, since a common divine source or a shared true history would explain the overlap. Some alleged sources, such as Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer for the raven, may postdate Islam, which would reverse the direction of borrowing. And the Quran self-consciously corrects and reframes these accounts: on the Sleepers, 18:22 rebukes speculation about the number, which shows critical engagement rather than credulous copying. On 5:32, they argue that Allah confirming a truth he originally inspired to Israel's sages is no embarrassment, since the verse explicitly says the decree was given to the Children of Israel.
quran-borrowed-legends.rationale: The dating defence fails where it matters most. Mishnah Sanhedrin was redacted about 200 AD, Genesis Rabbah by the 5th century, and the Seven Sleepers is firmly pre-Islamic in Jacob of Serugh. Those three are secure, whatever one says about Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer. The 'divine confirmation' move cannot rescue 5:32, because what the Quran presents as Allah's decree is identifiably a rabbi's exegetical inference from Hebrew grammar, drawn from the plural 'bloods of your brother'. And the Sleepers is a legend about the reign of Decius, not scripture. The correction at 18:22 concedes that the story arrived as circulating folklore. No Muslim response explains why revelation reproduces commentary.

houris-material-paradise.claim: The Quran's paradise is insistently sensual. There are wide-eyed maidens 'whom no man or jinn has touched' (55:56, 74), virgins made 'devoted, of equal age' for the companions of the right (56:35-38), 'full-breasted maidens of equal age' (78:33, kawa'ib atraban), along with wine, couches and served boys. The hadith intensify it. The martyr is 'married to seventy-two wives among the houris' (Jami at-Tirmidhi 1663, graded hasan sahih by Tirmidhi). Each man receives wives with marrow visible through their flesh, in a pearl tent sixty miles wide (Sahih al-Bukhari 3243). IslamQA 60188 affirms the houris as literal wives given for sexual enjoyment. Jesus taught the opposite: in the resurrection 'they neither marry nor are given in marriage' (Matthew 22:30), and heaven's centre is God himself dwelling with his people (Revelation 21:3; 22:4; Psalm 16:11). The contrast exposes what each faith holds as the ultimate good — reward, or God.
houris-material-paradise.response: IslamQA 60188 replies that critics caricature paradise. The Quran itself says 'the pleasure of Allah is greater' than all of it (9:72), and sound hadith make the vision of Allah's face the supreme reward. Physical delights are real because humans are resurrected bodily, a point Christianity shares, with a wedding feast, a city and a renewed earth. They are also purified of sin, since there is 'no idle talk therein' (56:25). The number 72 comes from a single companion-chain that some scholars grade weaker, and renderings like 'full-breasted' for kawa'ib are contested. Believing wives, they note, are promised higher status than the houris.
houris-material-paradise.rationale: This is graded admitted because mainstream Islamic authority affirms the substance. IslamQA and classical tafsir teach literal houris as sexual companions, and Tirmidhi himself graded the 72-wives hadith hasan sahih. The 9:72 rejoinder is fair as far as it goes, since Islam does hold Allah's pleasure supreme. But it does not erase the fact that the Quran's dominant, repeated portrait of reward is virgins, couches and wine, while God's own presence with his people — the engine of biblical hope from Eden to Revelation — is structurally marginal. The evangelistic point stands on Islam's own affirmed doctrine, not on polemical exaggeration.

women-testimony-inheritance.claim: Quran 2:282 requires two women to replace one male witness, 'so that if one errs, the other can remind her', and 4:11 fixes a daughter's inheritance at half a son's. Muhammad drew the theological conclusion himself: 'Is not the witness of a woman equal to half that of a man?... This is because of the deficiency of a woman's mind' (Sahih al-Bukhari 2658). In Sahih al-Bukhari 304 he declares women 'deficient in intelligence and religion' and 'the majority of the dwellers of Hell-fire'. These are not fringe readings. Classical fiqh built evidentiary and inheritance law on them, and they remain live in sharia codes today. Scripture's trajectory is different in kind. Male and female are jointly God's image (Genesis 1:27). The risen Christ's first commissioned witnesses were women (Luke 24:9-11), whose testimony was legally worthless in that culture and was preserved anyway. And in Christ 'there is no male and female' (Galatians 3:28).
women-testimony-inheritance.response: IslamQA 111867 and classical commentators explain the 'deficiency' as domain-specific rather than essential. The testimony rule concerns financial contracts that women then rarely handled, so a second woman guards against error born of inexperience. The 'religion' deficiency refers only to exemption from prayer and fasting during menstruation, which is an excused lack and not a culpable one. Inheritance halves reflect economics, not worth, since men bear mandatory financial responsibility for women through the mahr and full family maintenance; a sister's unencumbered half can exceed a brother's encumbered whole. Modern Muslim scholars add that 2:282 is context-bound commercial procedure, and note other testimony contexts where a woman's word stands alone (24:6-9).
women-testimony-inheritance.rationale: The texts and their operative legal force are undisputed; the defences reinterpret motive, not content. And the softening glosses collide with the sources themselves. Bukhari 2658 grounds the testimony rule in 'deficiency of mind', not in commercial inexperience, and the economics defence does not touch 'majority of the dwellers of Hell-fire'. Classical fiqh applied the half-witness rule far beyond finance, and states applying sharia apply it now. Because the substance is affirmed by Islam's most authentic hadith and by mainstream fatwa bodies, this is admitted. The honest debate is only over whether the arrangement is demeaning, which the texts' own stated rationale settles.

fatiha-daily-prayer-jews-christians.claim: Every observant Muslim recites Surah al-Fatiha in each unit of the five daily prayers, which is at minimum seventeen times daily. It closes with a plea to be guided in the path of those God favoured, 'not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who go astray' (1:7). Muhammad himself identified the referents: 'Those who have earned the anger are the Jews, and those who are led astray are the Christians' (Jami at-Tirmidhi 2954, graded hasan, from Adi ibn Hatim). Ibn Kathir records that 'the scholars of tafsir' held this view, citing broad early consensus, and it stands in Tafsir al-Jalalayn and in mainstream Salafi teaching today. So the world's second-largest religion liturgically defines itself, dozens of times a day, against Jews and Christians by name. Contrast the New Testament's posture toward those outside: 'love your enemies and pray for them' (Matthew 5:44), and Paul's 'my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved' (Romans 10:1).
fatiha-daily-prayer-jews-christians.response: Many Muslim teachers argue that the verse names categories, not ethnicities. 'Those who earned anger' are all who know truth and abandon it; 'those astray' are all who strive without knowledge. Jews and Christians appear in the hadith as historical exemplars, not as exclusive targets, and Muslims who fit the descriptions are equally included. The prayer, they stress, is a positive petition for guidance and not a curse on anyone; nothing in it asks harm for Jews or Christians. Modern expositors, such as Najam Academy, note that the Quran elsewhere commends righteous People of the Book (3:113-115), so 1:7 cannot be a blanket condemnation.
fatiha-daily-prayer-jews-christians.rationale: The identification is Islam's own, from Muhammad's mouth in a hasan hadith, and endorsed by Ibn Kathir as the view of 'the scholars of tafsir'. The categorical reading is the modern softening, not the classical mainstream. It is graded admitted because the substance — that the canonical exegesis names Jews and Christians — is affirmed within Islamic tradition itself. The defence that it is exemplary rather than exhaustive is genuine, but it does not remove Jews and Christians from the referent. It universalises the condemnation while keeping them as its archetypes. For evangelism the point is posture: daily self-definition against the biblical communities, versus daily intercession for the lost.

hadith-chain-of-custody.claim: Almost all that Islam knows of Muhammad comes from hadith. They were first written down long after his death in 632. That includes how to pray, the five pillars, the age of Aisha, the events of his life, and even the story of how the Quran was gathered. Al-Bukhari died in 870. He is said to have sifted some 600,000 reports in circulation and kept about 7,000, counting repeats. So the Muslim community itself made up false reports on a vast scale for two centuries. Western scholars pressed the point. Ignaz Goldziher, Joseph Schacht and G. H. A. Juynboll showed that chains were improved and pushed back in time, and that 'common links' point to chains made up whole. The trap for dawah is simple. If the hadith cannot be trusted, Islam cannot say its own prayers, fix its pillars, or tell its prophet's life, and the Quran floats free of context. If they can be trusted, then Bukhari's hard reports stand too: Aisha at nine, the spell, Banu Qurayza, and 'deficient in mind'. The Gospels, by contrast, were written while eyewitnesses lived, a fraction of that gap.
hadith-chain-of-custody.response: Muslim scholars answer that this is the most careful checking system in history. Each narrator was weighed by his life story, in the science called ilm al-rijal. Chains were cross-checked. Reports carried by large numbers are held to be certain. Muhammad Mustafa al-Azami and Harald Motzki showed that Schacht's dating went too far. Early written notes, such as the sahifa of Hammam ibn Munabbih, push the paper trail back near the first generation. Motzki's method, which reads chain and text together, verifies material Schacht threw out. Jonathan Brown notes that the tradition catalogued false reports itself, with a care Western critics only later found. And the 600,000 figure counts chain-variants, not separate lies.
hadith-chain-of-custody.rationale: The Muslim defence is serious work, but it sharpens the trap rather than escaping it. Every rescue of hadith reliability re-authenticates Bukhari's most damaging contents, which the same writers play down elsewhere. And every appeal to weak chains or context against those reports saws off the branch Islamic practice sits on. The gap with the New Testament is one of size and of kind. It is 25 to 60 years against 150 to 250. It is continuous writing against chains held in memory. And it is public events that hostile witnesses could check. As a structured dilemma, parallel to this site's tahrif centrepiece, it has no published Muslim answer that keeps both consistency and orthodoxy.

mariya-hafsa-surah-66.claim: Surah 66 opens with Allah rebuking Muhammad: 'O Prophet, why do you prohibit what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking the approval of your wives?' (66:1). It then dissolves his oath (66:2) and warns his wives that if he divorces them Allah will give him better ones (66:5). Sunan an-Nasa'i 3959, graded sahih by al-Albani, supplies the occasion. Muhammad 'had intercourse with' his slave woman, identified in tafsir as Mariya the Copt, in Hafsa's quarters or on her day. Aisha and Hafsa pressed him until he swore Mariya forbidden to himself, whereupon revelation descended freeing him from the oath. An alternative sahih occasion, in Sahih al-Bukhari 4912, involves only honey. Either way the shape matches the Zaynab pattern this site already covers. Heaven steps in, promptly and exactly, to release Muhammad from a bind at home. That is precisely what Aisha noted dryly: 'your Lord hastens to fulfill your wishes'.
mariya-hafsa-surah-66.response: Muslim scholars overwhelmingly prefer the honey account in Bukhari and Muslim as the surah's occasion, and Ask Ghamidi sets out the reasoning. Aisha herself narrates a jealous scheme about a honey drink at Zaynab's house, and the strongest-authenticated report should fix the context. The Mariya narrations, they argue, are aberrant, or shadhdh, or later conflated accounts. And even if some chain is technically sound, occasion-of-revelation reports are notoriously fluid. On the substance, the surah shows Muhammad's humanity and Allah's correction — he is rebuked, not indulged. And the principle established, that one may not make the lawful unlawful by oath, is sober jurisprudence, with expiation prescribed (66:2), matching Quran 5:89.
mariya-hafsa-surah-66.rationale: This is graded contested honestly. The honey narration is the better-attested occasion, and Christians should not overclaim the Mariya version — though al-Albani's sahih grading of Nasa'i 3959 means Muslims cannot simply wave it away either. But even on the most favourable Muslim reading, the pattern stands on the Quran's face. A chapter of eternal scripture is devoted to friction in the household, dissolving his oath and threatening his wives with replacement (66:5). Combined with 33:37 and 33:50-51, already in this app, it exhibits revelation repeatedly bending toward the prophet's personal convenience. The cumulative case, not the single incident, carries the evangelistic weight.

safiyya-khaybar-marriage.claim: At Khaybar in 628 AD the Muslims killed Kinana ibn al-Rabi. His wife was Safiyya bint Huyayy, a Jewish noblewoman of seventeen. Ibn Ishaq adds that Kinana was first burned to make him reveal treasure, then beheaded (Guillaume, page 515). Her father had already been killed with Banu Qurayza. Safiyya was taken captive and first given to Dihya al-Kalbi, then given to Muhammad (Sahih al-Bukhari 4200). Sahih al-Bukhari 371 records that he took her as wife on the journey home, at Sidd as-Sahba, days after her husband died. The companions asked aloud whether she was wife or slave. Islamic sources present this as honour. The plain sequence is that her husband and father were killed, and she was married within the week. There was no room for free consent, and the mourning rules were set aside. Set this against the test Jesus gave: 'by their fruits you will know them' (Matthew 7:16).
safiyya-khaybar-marriage.response: Al Hakam and other Muslim writers reply that Safiyya was honoured, not wronged. Muhammad freed her and made her freedom her mahr, raising a captive to be a Mother of the Believers. Later reports show her expressing love for him and defending him. Kinana died, they argue, for breaking the surrender terms by hiding treasure, which was a treaty violation. The burning detail rests on Ibn Ishaq's chainless report rather than on sahih hadith. Her marriage protected her, in a world where a defeated noblewoman had no better outcome. The consummation followed her purification, or istibra, which satisfied the waiting rule for captives. And Al Hakam argues that her consent is recorded.
safiyya-khaybar-marriage.rationale: The core sequence is Bukhari, not polemic. The husband was killed at Khaybar. Safiyya was taken from the captives. The marriage was consummated on the return journey. Only the burning detail depends on the sira alone. The defences concede every load-bearing fact and recast them as generosity. But her husband and father were killed by the same force, and she was offered marriage or captivity. That is not consent in any meaningful sense. And 'honour' assumes the captivity system itself is legitimate (Quran 33:50). This is graded admitted, since Islamic sources affirm the substance. The dispute is only over whether it was praiseworthy — which is exactly the question about character that this category exists to pose.

mutah-temporary-marriage.claim: Sahih hadith establish that Muhammad permitted mut'ah, a marriage contracted for a fixed term and payment that dissolves automatically. Companions on campaign were allowed to marry women 'for a fixed time', even for a garment (Sahih Muslim 1404), and Jabir reports that the practice continued through Abu Bakr's reign until Umar banned it (Sahih Muslim 1405). Sunni Islam holds that Muhammad finally prohibited it (Sahih al-Bukhari 5115; Sahih Muslim 1406, 'Allah has forbidden it until the Day of Resurrection'), though the abrogation is variously dated to Khaybar, to the conquest of Mecca, or to Umar's caliphate. Shia Islam rejects the abrogation, grounds the practice in Quran 4:24 — 'give them their due compensation for what you have enjoyed' — and practises mut'ah today, where in documented cases it functions as religiously laundered prostitution. Either Muhammad sanctioned term-limited sexual contracts, or the community that transmitted his religion cannot agree on what he finally commanded. Both horns matter against 'a marriage covenant witnessed by God' (Malachi 2:14).
mutah-temporary-marriage.response: IslamQA 20738 gives the Sunni answer. Mut'ah belongs to Islam's gradualist pedagogy, like the phased prohibition of alcohol. It was permitted briefly under wartime hardship, then abrogated by the Prophet himself 'until the Day of Resurrection' (Sahih Muslim 1406), with the four Sunni schools unanimous on its prohibition. So Islam cannot be charged with what it abolished, and Umar's ban merely enforced the Prophet's ruling. Shia scholars answer the opposite. Quran 4:24 sanctions it, no abrogating verse exists, and Umar had no authority to forbid what Muhammad allowed. Regulated mut'ah, with dower, term and idda, is a lawful institution and not prostitution.
mutah-temporary-marriage.rationale: This is graded contested because the Sunni abrogation defence is a genuine, well-sourced internal answer. Bukhari and Muslim do record prohibition, and it would be unfair to charge Sunni Islam with a practice it anathematises. But the challenge is not fully answered. Muhammad undeniably permitted term-limited sexual contracts for some period, which both sects agree on, and that is itself the moral datum against the biblical vision of marriage. The abrogation chronology is internally tangled. And a quarter of the Muslim world's second-largest branch practises mut'ah now, on Quranic grounds Sunnis cannot conclusively rebut without appealing to Umar's authority. The disagreement also feeds the hadith-epistemology entry, since the two communities' canons yield opposite final rulings.

kaaba-black-stone-pagan-rites.claim: Islam's central rites predate Islam. The Kaaba was a functioning pagan shrine housing 360 idols until Muhammad cleansed it in 630 (Sahih al-Bukhari 4287). Pre-Islamic Arabs already performed tawaf, venerated the Black Stone, and ran between Safa and Marwa — a rite associated with the idols Isaf and Na'ila, which the Quran had to expressly re-authorise (2:158). Muslims still kiss or salute the embedded Black Stone. Umar's unease is canonical: 'I know that you are a stone and can neither benefit nor harm. Had I not seen the Prophet kissing you, I would not have kissed you' (Sahih al-Bukhari 1597). Other hadith give the stone unusual powers. It came down from paradise whiter than milk. Sins turned it black. It will testify on judgment day (Jami at-Tirmidhi 877, 961). So there is a question for a faith that defines itself against idols. Why does its holiest act keep a pagan shrine's stone-kissing circuit, unchanged in form?
kaaba-black-stone-pagan-rites.response: IslamQA 118085 answers that the direction of history is reversed. Abraham and Ishmael built the Kaaba for pure monotheism (Quran 2:127), and the pagan rites were later corruptions of an originally Abrahamic pilgrimage. So Islam did not adopt paganism; it stripped paganism off an ancient monotheist sanctuary and restored the original. Kissing the stone, IslamQA explains, is pure ittiba', following the Prophet's example, and explicitly not worship. Umar's statement is cited by Muslims themselves as proof that the act carries no belief in the stone's power. Tawaf and Safa-Marwa commemorate Abrahamic history, including Hagar's search for water, re-sanctified by revelation.
kaaba-black-stone-pagan-rites.rationale: This is graded contested, conservatively. The link between the rites and pre-Islamic paganism is a matter of Islamic record. Bukhari 4287 supplies the idols, and the fresh permission at 2:158 assumes the pagan tie. And the 'Abrahamic original' has no support from before Islam. It depends wholly on the Quran's assertion, while the Ishmael entry shows Genesis places Abraham nowhere near Mecca. But the Muslim intent-distinction is real. Mainstream Islam explicitly denies the stone any power, and Umar's canonical statement functions as an internal anti-idolatry guardrail. So the strong claim, that Muslims worship a stone, fails. The fair claim stands: Islam's central rite is a retained pagan circuit resting on an unevidenced origin story.

sword-verses-final-command.claim: Surah 9, by Muslim consensus among the last revealed, commands 'kill the polytheists wherever you find them' after the sacred months (9:5), and 'fight those who do not believe in Allah... from the People of the Book until they pay the jizya with willing submission, and feel themselves subdued' (9:29). Under Islam's own abrogation doctrine, later revelation governs earlier. Ibn Kathir's tafsir records Ad-Dahhak's judgment that the Verse of the Sword 'abrogated every agreement of peace between the Prophet and any idolator, every treaty, and every term'. Classical jurists across the schools built offensive-jihad doctrine on exactly this chronology, and Muhammad's own summary is canonical: 'I have been ordered to fight the people until they say: none has the right to be worshipped but Allah' (Sahih al-Bukhari 25). The frequently quoted 'no compulsion in religion' (2:256) is Medinan but earlier, which is why the classical tradition, not Islamophobes, treated the sword verses as operative. Jesus's final commands run the other direction: 'put your sword back' (Matthew 26:52), and 'make disciples... teaching them' (Matthew 28:19-20).
sword-verses-final-command.response: Discover The Truth and other Muslim scholars answer that context confines both verses. Quran 9:1-4 addresses pagan tribes who violated their treaties; 9:4 explicitly exempts those who kept terms, and 9:6 commands escorting an enemy who seeks protection to safety. Quran 9:29 concerns hostile Byzantine-aligned powers ahead of Tabuk, not all Christians everywhere. The sweeping abrogation claims are attributed to individual exegetes rather than to consensus. Many classical scholars, and nearly all modern ones, hold 2:256 and 60:8 un-abrogated, making jihad defensive or state-conducted and never vigilante. And Bukhari 25's 'the people' is read as the specific treaty-breaking Arab polytheists, in line with the parallel narrations.
sword-verses-final-command.rationale: Contested is the honest grade. The contextual defence has genuine textual anchors in 9:4 and 9:6, and painting all Islam with Ad-Dahhak's maximalism would be the mirror error of Muslim apologists' minimalism. What the defence cannot dissolve is 9:29. It targets People of the Book as such, prescribing fighting until tribute and subjugation — a command that classical fiqh of every school operationalised for a millennium of expansionist jurisprudence. The contextual reading is historically the reformist position, not the classical one. The evangelistic use is precise, not polemical: ask which trajectory each founder's final commands set. This entry deliberately complements, without duplicating, the sharia and spread-by-sword entries.

muhammad-bewitched.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 3268, narrated by Aisha, reports that a Jewish sorcerer, Labid ibn al-A'sam, worked magic on Muhammad using his hair and a comb, 'so that he began to imagine that he had done a thing which he had not really done'. By some accounts the state lasted months. Sahih Muslim 2189 carries the same account, so it is as authenticated as hadith get. The problem is double. Internally, the Quran indignantly denies the charge that Muhammad was 'a bewitched man' (17:47; 25:8), yet Islam's most authentic hadith affirm exactly that. And there is a deeper problem about knowledge. A prophet whose mind could be made to experience things that never happened, by a hostile magician, for an extended period during his revelatory career, has no way to certify which of his experiences were genuine. The biblical test excludes this outright, since God's true prophet is not overpowered by sorcery — 'there is no enchantment against Jacob' (Numbers 23:23) — and God's word does not come through a compromised channel (Deuteronomy 18:21-22).
muhammad-bewitched.response: IslamQA 68814, SeekersGuidance and mainstream commentators respond that the magic affected only Muhammad's worldly, domestic life. The classical example is his imagining he had approached his wives when he had not. It never touched revelation, whose integrity Allah guarantees (5:67; 15:9). It was an illness like any bodily ailment prophets suffer. It ended in a miracle, since Allah revealed the spell's location and cure, as the hadith itself reports, with Surahs 113 and 114 linked to the deliverance. And 25:8's denial concerns the pagans' charge that the Quran itself was the product of sorcery, which is a different claim from the prophet suffering a temporary spell. Some early scholars and modernists simply rejected the report as contradicting the Quran.
muhammad-bewitched.rationale: The 'worldly matters only' firewall is asserted, never demonstrated. The hadith's own description — believing he had done what he had not done — is a defect of perception and memory, the exact faculties revelation depends on. No criterion is offered by which Muhammad or anyone else could separate bewitched experiences from genuine ones. And the minority who reject the report to save the Quran, which is a live Muslim position, impale themselves on the hadith-epistemology dilemma. Bukhari's most rigorously authenticated Aisha material would fall, and Islamic method would fall with it. The internal tension with 25:8 is answered only by redescribing the pagans' charge. No resolution holds all three: sahih hadith, Quranic denial, and prophetic reliability.

sins-cast-on-jews-christians.claim: Sahih Muslim preserves a startling soteriology. 'When it is the Day of Resurrection, Allah will deliver to every Muslim a Jew or a Christian and say: That is your rescue from Hell-Fire' (Sahih Muslim 2767a). The companion narrations are stronger still. Muslims will arrive 'with sins like mountains', and Allah will forgive the Muslims 'and place them on the Jews and Christians' instead. And: 'No Muslim dies but Allah admits in his stead a Jew or a Christian in Hell-Fire' (Sahih Muslim 2767b). This is substitutionary atonement inverted. The one innocent of those sins is damned in place of the guilty, by religious category, without consent, justice or love. The gospel's substitution is its precise mirror, since the sinless one voluntarily bears sin for the guilty — 'He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree' (1 Peter 2:24), 'the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world' (John 1:29). Every human heart senses that guilt must go somewhere. The two religions answer with opposite substitutes.
sins-cast-on-jews-christians.response: IslamQA 9488 explains that the unbelievers are not punished for the Muslims' sins, since that would contradict 'no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another' (6:164). Rather, the Jew or Christian enters Hell for his own disbelief. 'Ransom', or fida', is figurative. Each person has a place in Paradise and a place in Hell. When a Muslim is forgiven, the unbeliever inherits the vacated place in Hell that his own sins already earned, just as the Muslim inherits his place in Paradise, per the parallel in Muslim's collection. Al-Nawawi's commentary takes the wording as a metaphor for the fixed populations of the two abodes, so no injustice occurs.
sins-cast-on-jews-christians.rationale: The hadith are sahih Muslim material, and IslamQA's harmonisation concedes that the wording needs rescuing. The 'inherited places' reading must flatly re-explain the sentence in which Allah forgives the Muslims and places their sins on the Jews and Christians, which states transfer, not vacancy. Even granting Al-Nawawi's metaphor, the admitted picture remains. Muslims with mountain-sized sins are forgiven, not through any atonement, but by category membership, while Jews and Christians serve as their counterweight. That is mercy without a ground, at the expense of justice, which is precisely the problem the cross answers (Romans 3:26). It is graded admitted since the texts and their canonical status are affirmed, and only the mechanics are debated. This is a powerful and underused bridge to substitution rightly understood.

uzair-son-of-god.claim: Quran 9:30 asserts as fact: 'The Jews say: Ezra (Uzair) is the son of Allah.' It is set in parallel with the Christian confession of Christ, and Allah's curse is pronounced on both groups for it. But no Jewish text, sect or tradition in the entire historical record calls Ezra the son of God. Not the Tanakh, the Talmud, the Mishnah, Philo, Josephus, Qumran, or any rabbinic source. Judaism's defining confession is the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4), and deifying a scribe would be its ultimate blasphemy. Historians call the verse enigmatic precisely because the belief is unattested. The error matters doubly for dawah. An omniscient author does not misreport the theology of a community living in Medina alongside Muhammad. And the verse's symmetry — 'and the Christians say the Messiah is the son of Allah' — shows the Quran treating both sonship claims as parallel human inventions, misunderstanding the Christian claim it means to refute.
uzair-son-of-god.response: Muslim commentators from al-Tabari onward answer that the verse reports a claim of some Jews, not all. Classical tafsir names individual Medinan Jews, such as Finhas. Others name a Yemeni or Arabian Jewish faction who honoured Ezra as restorer of the Torah, to the point of calling him Allah's son. Arabic, they say, permits attributing a subgroup's saying to the group. IslamQA 164633 adds that the absence from surviving Jewish literature proves little, since a small Arabian sect would leave no rabbinic paper trail. And some modern Muslim writers point to the exalted Ezra of 4 Ezra, or to the deified-scribe traditions around Enoch and Metatron, as the kind of setting the Quran could be indicting.
uzair-son-of-god.rationale: The defence is an argument from silence about a sect for which the only evidence is the verse needing rescue. That is circular. The classical commentators also conflict with each other — one man, one delegation, a Yemeni sect. That shows they possessed no actual historical referent. 4 Ezra and the Metatron traditions never call Ezra God's son, and they belong to different figures and genres. The verse generalises, 'the Jews say', exactly as it does for Christians, where the Quran means the mainstream confession, so the subgroup reading is special pleading. As with the Mary-in-the-Trinity entry already in this app, the pattern is a polemicist misreporting his neighbours' beliefs, not omniscience.

allah-name-polemic.claim: A popular evangelical polemic claims that 'Allah' is intrinsically the name of a false deity, so Muslims linguistically worship someone other than the biblical God, and Christians must never use the word. The evidence is against the linguistic claim. 'Allah' is simply Arabic for God, from al-ilah, 'the God', and it is cognate with Hebrew Eloah and Elohim and with Aramaic Alaha — likely close to what Jesus's own Aramaic-speaking circle called God. Arab Christians used it before Muhammad existed. The trilingual Zabad inscription of 512 AD, on a church of St Sergius, opens its Arabic line invoking al-ilah. Pre-Islamic Christian Arab tribes prayed to Allah, and every Arabic Bible from the earliest translations to today renders 'God' as 'Allah'. Millions of Arab Christians confess Allah as Father, Son and Holy Spirit every Sunday. The real issue is conceptual, not lexical.
allah-name-polemic.response: Muslim apologists happily agree with the linguistic facts and press them further. Since Allah is the God of Abraham by name and heritage, and Quran 29:46 instructs Muslims to tell the People of the Book 'our God and your God is one', Christians who concede the shared name should concede a shared God, differing only in later corruptions such as the Trinity. On this footing Islam presents itself as the purification of Abrahamic monotheism rather than a rival deity's cult. Dawah regularly cites Arab Christian usage of 'Allah' as evidence that Islam worships the same God Christians do, merely more consistently.
allah-name-polemic.rationale: This is graded answered. The polemic's factual core is simply wrong, and Muslim and Arab Christian sources answer it decisively, since 'Allah' predates Islam as the Arabic word for God and is used in Christian inscriptions and in every Arabic Bible. Christians who lead with it lose credibility with any Arabic-speaking hearer in the first minute. The entry's value is triage: drop the lexical argument, keep the conceptual one. Whether the Quran's Allah — a non-triune monad who is not Father, has no Son, and saves without atonement — accurately describes the God of Abraham is the real question, and this app's doctrine-of-god and tahrif entries prosecute it on ground that actually holds.

first-revelation-terror.claim: By Islam's own most trusted sources, Muhammad's first encounter with revelation left him terrified and unable to identify its source. In Aisha's long narration (Sahih al-Bukhari 3, repeated at 6982), the being in the cave of Hira seized and squeezed him three times. He fled to Khadijah trembling, crying 'Cover me! Cover me!' and confessing 'I fear that something may happen to me.' Ibn Ishaq's sirah, Islam's earliest biography, records his own first hypotheses as the worst available: 'ecstatic poet or a man possessed... Woe is me' (Guillaume, Life of Muhammad, page 106). It took Khadijah and her cousin Waraqah bin Naufal — a Christian conversant with prior scripture — to pronounce the visitor divine. Sahih al-Bukhari 6982 then describes the fatra, the pause in revelation, during which, 'as we have heard', he grieved so deeply that he repeatedly 'intended to throw himself from the tops of high mountains'. Contrast Isaiah 6, Jeremiah 1 and Luke 1: fear is present, but God self-identifies, and the angel's first word is 'Fear not.'
first-revelation-terror.response: Mahajjah, a traditional Sunni scholarship portal, answers that terror is precisely what a genuine encounter with the transcendent produces. Moses fled from the sign at the bush (Quran 28:31). Fear also argues for sincerity, since an impostor invents a flattering commissioning, not one that leaves him suspecting madness. The mountain-tops line, they stress, is not Aisha's testimony at all. Ibn Hajar, in Fath al-Bari, identifies it as a balagh of al-Zuhri, introduced by fima balaghana, 'as we have heard', transmitted only in Ma'mar's recension and absent from those of 'Uqayl and Yunus. It is a disconnected report carrying no sahih weight. Waraqah's role is read as providence: a scholar of previous revelation recognising the same Namus, or angel, who came to Moses, which confirms continuity rather than supplying legitimacy Muhammad lacked.
first-revelation-terror.rationale: This is graded admitted because every load-bearing fact sits in Islam's own canon and is undisputed: the terror, 'Cover me', 'I fear for myself', and the need for Waraqah, a Christian, to certify the encounter as divine (Bukhari 3 and 6982; Muslim 160). Honesty requires conceding the strongest Muslim point, and this site does. The suicidal-despair line is weak by Islam's own hadith science, resting on al-Zuhri's unattributed addendum via Ma'mar alone, so do not build the argument on it. Build it on what no one disputes. The recipient of the revelation could not himself identify its source, and the identification came from a human being. Biblical commissioning scenes carry divine self-identification, and Paul's warning about 'an angel from heaven' preaching another gospel frames the stakes (Galatians 1:8). The severity is high, because 'how do you know it was Gabriel?' touches the foundation of everything downstream.

quran-262-vs-385.claim: Quran 2:62 promises that 'those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians — whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day and did righteousness — will have their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them'. Quran 5:69 repeats the promise nearly verbatim. Yet Quran 3:85 declares: 'Whoever desires other than Islam as religion — never will it be accepted from him, and he, in the Hereafter, will be among the losers' (compare 3:19). The classical resolution concedes the tension. Al-Tabari's tafsir on 2:62 records Ibn Abbas saying the verse was abrogated by 3:85, though Mujahid and al-Dahhak held 2:62 muhkama, still standing, and al-Tabari himself preferred a restricted reading. Sahih Muslim 153 seals the exclusivist position, since any Jew or Christian who hears of Muhammad and dies without believing his message 'will be among the inhabitants of the Fire'. Modern scholars split between abrogation and restriction. Either way the two texts pull in opposite directions, and the abrogation solution is itself an admission of it.
quran-262-vs-385.response: Most Muslim exegetes deny any contradiction, and the Yaqeen Institute sets out the case. On the majority reading, 2:62 addresses Jews, Christians and Sabians who lived faithfully before Muhammad, or who accept him once his message reaches them. 'Whoever believed in Allah and the Last Day' is read as belief on Islam's own terms, which after 610 AD includes Muhammad's prophethood. Others note that when Ibn Abbas said naskh he frequently meant takhsis, specification, rather than repeal, so 3:85 clarifies the scope of 2:62 rather than cancelling a salvation once offered. On this view the verses teach one consistent doctrine across time: every era's believers must follow the prophet sent to them, and after Muhammad that means Islam. The Quran, they argue, elsewhere criticises Jews and Christians precisely for failing their own covenants, so 2:62 was never a blanket pluralism.
quran-262-vs-385.rationale: This is graded contested, not unrefuted, because the restriction reading is a coherent harmonisation the Arabic can bear, and it was held by classical authorities including Mujahid, al-Dahhak and arguably al-Tabari himself. This site does not overclaim. But the argument retains real force. The harmonisation must be imported, since nothing in 2:62's wording limits it to a past era. The abrogation report preserved in Islam's own premier tafsir concedes that the earliest readers felt the collision. And Sahih Muslim 153 makes the operative doctrine unambiguous. The evangelistic use is not a gotcha but clarity. A Muslim friend citing 2:62 as proof that Islam honours Christians should know that their own tradition denies that Christians who remain Christians are saved. Contrast the New Testament's single consistent claim (John 14:6; Acts 4:12) with a God 'with whom there is no variation' (James 1:17).

slavery-never-abolished.claim: Islamic law softened slavery but never ended it. The Quran makes captive women lawful to their captors — 'and prohibited to you are married women, except those your right hands possess' (4:24; compare 33:50). Freeing a slave earns reward (Sahih al-Bukhari 2517), and papers of release are urged (24:33). Yet owning a slave stayed lawful in every classical school. By the sahih sources, Muhammad owned, bought, sold and freed slaves. He bought a slave for two black slaves (Sahih Muslim 1602). He took captives from Banu Mustaliq (Sahih al-Bukhari 2541). He held Mariyah the Copt as a concubine. No Muslim state ended slavery from within sharia. The end came under Western and colonial pressure. Saudi Arabia in 1962. Oman in 1970. Mauritania in 1981, the last country on earth, and a crime there only from 2007, with campaign groups still finding cases. In 2014 ISIS brought back sex slavery of Yazidi women, announced in Dabiq issue 4 as 'The Revival of Slavery Before the Hour', citing classical fiqh directly. The law of Moses, by contrast, set rules with release built in. There was release in the seventh year (Exodus 21:2), death for stealing a man (Exodus 21:16), and shelter rather than return for an escaped slave (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). And the movement that ended the trade was led mostly by Christians, through Wilberforce and the Quakers.
slavery-never-abolished.response: IslamQA 94840 defends slow release and direction of travel. Islam inherited a world economy built on slaves and turned it toward freedom. Freeing a slave pays for a broken oath and other sins. It is one of the set uses of zakat (9:60), and among the most praised acts of piety. Masters must feed and clothe slaves as themselves. The mukataba contract (24:33) let slaves buy their freedom. Muhammad freed slaves, and raised one, Zayd, to be his adopted son and an army commander. Modern scholars add that treaty duties bind under sharia. So the treaties that ended slavery bind Muslim states too, and the slave-raiding of groups like ISIS breaks that consensus. On this account the method was freedom by attrition, and abolition fulfils the intent rather than opposing it.
slavery-never-abolished.rationale: This is graded admitted because the core facts are conceded on all sides. IslamQA affirms today that slavery was never forbidden by sharia. The direction-of-travel defence explains the softening. It does not explain the thirteen centuries in which no school and no state took the last step. Nor why the end arrived only under outside pressure. Nor why ISIS could cite mainstream classical fiqh rather than fringe texts. Be honest about the Bible. The law of Moses also set rules for slavery rather than ending it, and Christians long misused Scripture to defend it. The difference is direction. There are release rules, the death penalty for man-stealing, Deuteronomy's shelter for those who run, and Philemon's 'no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother'. And the movement that ended it was driven by Christian conviction. Use this comparison carefully, and concede Christian failures first. The argument is strongest when it stays about texts and legal systems, not about whose ancestors behaved better.

fgm-classical-fiqh.claim: Classical Islamic law addresses female circumcision, and one school mandated it. The Shafi'i manual Umdat al-Salik, or Reliance of the Traveller, rules at e4.3 that circumcision is obligatory, wajib, for both sexes, and its English edition was certified by al-Azhar. It describes the female form as cutting the prepuce of the clitoris, with translation disputes over whether the Arabic bazr means the prepuce or the clitoris itself. Hanbalis were split between obligatory and honourable. Hanafis and Malikis called it recommended or noble, a makrumah, and not required. IslamQA's current answer 60314 still defends the practice as part of the fitrah. The main supporting hadith is Umm Atiyyah's, in which Muhammad says 'do not cut severely, as that is better for a woman and more desirable for a husband' (Sunan Abi Dawud 5271). Abu Dawud himself declared it weak, 'not strong', and mursal, as did al-Iraqi and al-Azimabadi, though al-Albani later authenticated it via corroborating chains. Practice tracks madhhab geography — Shafi'i Southeast Asia, Egypt, the Horn of Africa — but the custom predates Islam and exists among non-Muslims in those regions. The 2006 al-Azhar conference condemned FGM as criminal aggression, and Grand Mufti Ali Gomaa's 2007 fatwa forbade it.
fgm-classical-fiqh.response: Muslim scholars opposing the practice argue the case from inside the tradition. The Umm Atiyyah hadith is weak by Abu Dawud's own assessment, so no obligation can be built on it. Nothing in the Quran addresses the practice at all. And the sharia's governing principle of la darar, no harm, forbids any procedure that medicine shows to be injurious. The Fiqh Council of North America and Grand Mufti Ali Gomaa have ruled FGM prohibited outright, and the 2006 al-Azhar conference called it punishable aggression. Defenders of the classical position, meanwhile, insist the fiqh only ever sanctioned a minimal symbolic cut — the 'do not cut severely' wording itself — and that severe forms such as infibulation are pre-Islamic African custom the jurists never endorsed, practised by Christians and animists in the same regions.
fgm-classical-fiqh.rationale: This is graded contested because the honest picture cuts both ways. The textual basis is weak, by Abu Dawud's own grading, and there is no Quranic support. Major Muslim authorities now prohibit the practice, and the custom is regional and pre-Islamic. Yet it remains true that classical fiqh canonised rather than abolished it, that one school made it obligatory, and that IslamQA defends it today. State every one of those clauses or state none. The pastoral guidance is emphatic. This topic is explosive and almost always counterproductive in personal evangelism. It exists in this database for completeness, and for the rare context where a Muslim friend has raised comparative arguments about women's status and expects candour in return. Never open with it. Never use it as a weapon. Lead with listening. A Muslim friend likely finds FGM as abhorrent as you do, and treating him as its defender is both unjust and conversation-ending.

quran-grammar-irregularities.claim: The Quran rests its great miracle on language nobody can match — 'produce a surah like it' (2:23) — in 'clear Arabic' (12:2). Yet classical scholars themselves listed odd forms. Arabic marks case by word endings. Quran 4:162 has al-muqimina, 'those who establish prayer', in one case while the nouns around it stand in another. Quran 5:69 has al-sabi'una in a form the particle inna should not allow, unlike 2:62 and 22:17, where the same word follows the rule. Quran 20:63 reads inna hadhani la-sahirani, where inna calls for hadhayni. Quran 2:177 does the same with al-sabirina. Early reports admit the problem. Uthman is said to have remarked of the compiled text, 'I see errors (lahn) in it, and the Arabs will correct them with their tongues.' And a report through Abu Ubayd's Fada'il al-Qur'an has Aisha judge that 4:162, 5:69 and 20:63 are 'the fault of the scribes'. Both reports are themselves disputed, since their chains are contested and Muslim scholars reject or reread them. Classical grammarians smoothed each verse by appeal to poetic licence, dialect and the praise form — which is itself a sign that the oddities were felt.
quran-grammar-irregularities.response: Muslim grammarians and modern academics, including Islamic Awareness, answer that these are attested classical Arabic and not errors. The form in 4:162 and 2:177 is the well-known qat' construction, used for praise, meaning 'and especially those who...', and it appears in pre-Islamic poetry. The form in 5:69 can be a delayed topic. And 20:63's hadhani matches the speech of certain Arab tribes, said to be Banu al-Harith, who keep the same dual form in every case. The earliest word scholars knew that reading. The Uthman and Aisha reports, they argue, are unreliable. Their chains are contested. Lahn in early usage could mean a style of reciting rather than an error. And it is hard to believe Uthman would standardise a text he thought faulty, while companions who had memorised it raised no objection. Grammar books were written after the Quran, and partly from it.
quran-grammar-irregularities.rationale: This is graded contested because the Muslim defences have real substance. Several forms do have parallels in old poetry and tribal speech. Grammar books came after the Quran. And the Uthman and Aisha reports carry disputed chains, so this site will not lean on reports it would reject if they favoured Islam. What survives is narrower but still notable. A book whose signature miracle is perfect language holds a handful of forms that needed generations of repair, dialect appeals and case-by-case pleading. And the earliest Muslims passed on reports alleging scribal error, which is not what a community sure of perfect wording tends to keep. Use this only with someone who cares about the i'jaz argument. It carries no weight with an ordinary Muslim friend and can look like nit-picking. Note too that Christianity claims God-breathed meaning through human authors (Luke 1:1-4), not dictated perfection of wording. The comparison of claims is the real point.

quran-65-4-child-iddah.claim: Quran 65:4 legislates the iddah, the waiting period after divorce, for three groups of wives, including those 'who have not menstruated'. The classical commentators — al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and the standard tafsir tradition — uniformly read this as girls who have not yet reached puberty. Since Quran 33:49 says no iddah exists at all for an unconsummated marriage, the verse presupposes consummated marriages to prepubescent girls. That embeds child marriage in the Quran's own divorce legislation, independently of the Aisha biography.
quran-65-4-child-iddah.response: Modern apologists, such as Discover The Truth, argue that 'those who have not menstruated' refers to adult women with delayed menarche or amenorrhea, not to children. They add that the verse addresses waiting periods generally without endorsing child marriage, and some note that a marriage contract does not imply consummation. This stands in contrast with the classical position in Ibn Kathir and in Ma'arif al-Qur'an, which state that the verse covers 'the young who have not reached the years of menstruation'.
quran-65-4-child-iddah.rationale: The delayed-menarche reading is a modern retrofit held by no classical authority. The tafsir tradition is unanimous that the clause covers the not-yet-pubescent, and the fiqh manuals of all four schools drew the corresponding rule. The iddah logic is the trap. Quran 33:49 removes any waiting period for unconsummated marriages, so an iddah for the never-menstruated only has work to do if such marriages were consummated. This is the legislative twin of the Aisha case. Even if every biographical report were discarded, the law would remain in the text.

four-witnesses-rape-standard.claim: Quran 24:4 requires four eyewitnesses to prove unlawful intercourse. An accuser who cannot produce them receives eighty lashes, and 24:13 applies the same test. Classical fiqh placed rape, zina-bil-jabr, under the rules of proof for zina. Pakistan wrote that into the 1979 Hudood Ordinance. The result is documented. Women who reported rape were prosecuted for zina, their complaint read as an admission of intercourse they could not prove was forced. It took secular law, the Women's Protection Act of 2006, to move rape out of that framework and back into the Penal Code.
four-witnesses-rape-standard.response: Muslims respond that the original purpose of 24:4 was protective, shielding women from casual accusations of adultery, since its occasion was the slander of Aisha. They add that rape could alternatively be prosecuted as hiraba, violent crime, without four witnesses. And they argue that the Hudood Ordinance was bad man-made legislation rather than true sharia — as shown by the Pakistani religious scholars who supported the 2006 reform. Both the reformist and traditional positions are surveyed in the Washington and Lee Law Review article on twenty-five years of the Hudood Ordinances and in the 2006 reform debate.
four-witnesses-rape-standard.rationale: The protective-intent point about slander is genuine and should be conceded. But the case is about downstream application. The classical manuals did apply zina's evidentiary bar to rape claims. The hiraba route was the minority workaround rather than the operative rule. And when a modern state implemented the classical framework, the predicted injustice occurred at scale for 27 years. The instructive contrast is Deuteronomy 22:25-27, which explicitly declares the rape victim innocent — 'to the young woman you shall do nothing' — with no witness quota imposed on her. As a usage note, lead with the Pakistan history, which is documented, and acknowledge 24:4's anti-slander context up front. It makes the argument stronger, not weaker.

iblis-angel-or-jinn.claim: Five times the Quran says the angels were commanded to prostrate to Adam, 'and they prostrated, except Iblis' (2:34; 7:11; 15:30-31; 20:116; 38:73-74). That is grammar which counts Iblis among the angels. But 18:50 says 'he was of the jinn, so he rebelled'. The Quran also says angels never disobey Allah (66:6), yet on the angel reading Iblis did exactly that. And Iblis says he was created from fire (7:12), while the hadith says angels were created from light and jinn from smokeless fire (Sahih Muslim 2996).
iblis-angel-or-jinn.response: The tafsir literature offers three classical harmonisations. Al-Tabari, following reports from Ibn Abbas, holds that Iblis belonged to a tribe of angels called 'jinn', guardians of Paradise, created from fire. Al-Hasan al-Basri, cited approvingly by Ibn Kathir, holds that Iblis 'was not an angel for the twinkling of an eye', and that the exception in 2:34 is a disconnected exception, meaning he was merely among the angels when the command came. Al-Baydawi holds that he was created an angel and became jinn by his deed.
iblis-angel-or-jinn.rationale: The tradition never settled it, and the rescues are mutually exclusive. Al-Tabari's 'angelic tribe called jinn' preserves the grammar of 2:34, but it collides with 66:6, since angels cannot disobey, and with the light-and-fire distinction. Al-Hasan al-Basri's 'never an angel' saves 18:50, but only by making the Quran's own repeated sentence structure misleading five times over. In conversation this is a clean, self-contained internal-consistency test that requires no external sources, only the Quran read carefully. Pick either horn and let the tafsir tradition supply the contradiction.

creation-six-or-eight-days.claim: Four passages say the heavens and earth were created in six days: 7:54, 10:3, 11:7 and 25:59. But 41:9-12 itemises the stages. The earth took two days. Then, thumma, mountains and provisions took four days. Then, thumma, the seven heavens took two days. Two plus four plus two is eight. There is a bonus tension as well. In 41:9-12 the earth is completed before the heavens, while 79:27-30 builds the heaven first and spreads the earth 'after that', ba'da dhalika.
creation-six-or-eight-days.response: The standard answer comes from IslamQA 31865, following Tafsir Ibn Kathir on 41:9-12. The 'four days' of 41:10 are inclusive. The earth was created in two days and its mountains and provisions in two more, so 'four days' means four in total up to that point. Four plus two is six.
creation-six-or-eight-days.rationale: The inclusive reading has to fight the text's own conjunction. Each stage is introduced with thumma, 'then', which in Arabic marks sequence rather than overlap. Nobody reads 'I built the house in two days, then finished the roof in four days' as six days total, except by special pleading. Translators sympathetic to the harmonisation must insert parenthetical glosses, such as 'four days including the former two', that are not in the Arabic. Note honestly if it is raised that Christians read Genesis's days in more than one way too. But Genesis's numbers at least add up.

qadar-created-for-hell.claim: The Quran teaches that Allah decrees everything, including belief and disbelief. 'We have created for Hell many of the jinn and mankind' (7:179). 'Whomever Allah leaves astray, none can guide' (7:178). 'Nothing will befall us except what Allah has decreed for us' (9:51). 'You do not will unless Allah wills' (76:30; 81:29). In Sahih al-Bukhari 6594 the angel writes each person's deeds, and whether he is 'doomed or blessed', before birth. Sahih al-Bukhari 6596 is titled 'The pen has dried'. So Allah creates people for Hell and then punishes them for what he decreed.
qadar-created-for-hell.response: Sunni orthodoxy answers with the Ash'ari doctrine of kasb, or acquisition. Allah creates every act, but the human 'acquires' it and so bears responsibility. Foreknowledge and the writing of it are not compulsion. And 32:13 — 'had We willed, We could have given every soul its guidance' — shows that guidance withheld is withheld justly. IslamQA 264354 frames this as a matter where reason must submit. Both the decree and human responsibility are affirmed, without full reconciliation.
qadar-created-for-hell.rationale: Kasb re-labels the problem rather than solving it. Muslim scholars themselves proverbially listed al-Ash'ari's kasb among the famously unintelligible doctrines. And the Quran's language is stronger than mere foreknowledge: created for Hell (7:179), 'I will surely fill Hell' (32:13), and Allah 'sends astray whom He wills' (14:4). The biblical contrast is the point for conversation. The God of Scripture 'takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked' (Ezekiel 33:11; compare 18:23), 'desires all people to be saved' (1 Timothy 2:4; 2 Peter 3:9), and pleads 'choose life' (Deuteronomy 30:19). Christians who debate sovereignty and freedom do so inside those constraints; the Quran removes them. Handle with care, since a Muslim may quote Calvinist material back. The answer is that no Christian tradition teaches that God delights in damnation, or creates men in order to damn them.

triple-talaq-halala.claim: Quran 2:230 says that after a third divorce a woman is not lawful to her husband again 'until she has married another husband'. Muhammad applied it literally. When Rifa'a's thrice-divorced wife wanted to return to him, he answered, 'No — not until he tastes your sweetness and you taste his sweetness' (Sahih al-Bukhari 5260), meaning the intervening marriage must be consummated. The rule generated halala, or tahleel — arranged one-night marriages to re-legalise a wife — a practice still sold as a service today. And instant triple talaq remained live law until Muslim-majority jurisdictions legislated against it. In India it was struck down in Shayara Bano in 2017 and criminalised in 2019.
triple-talaq-halala.response: Muslims respond on three fronts. First, a contracted halala — marrying with the prior intention of divorcing in order to re-legalise the woman — is itself cursed and invalid in the hadith, since the muhallil, 'the one who makes lawful', is condemned; see IslamQA 159041. Second, the rule in 2:230 is a deterrent, designed to make men take divorce seriously. Third, instant triple talaq in one sitting, talaq-e-biddat, is a condemned innovation and not original Islam.
triple-talaq-halala.rationale: The curse on the muhallil only forbids the arrangement being explicit. The underlying rule stands on any reading. A thrice-divorced woman cannot return to her husband until another man has consummated a marriage with her, and Sahih al-Bukhari 5260 puts the consummation requirement in Muhammad's own mouth. The 'deterrent' framing concedes the mechanism, since the deterrent's payload is the wife's sexual union with another man. The clandestine halala-service market, documented by the BBC in the UK and litigated in India, is the rule's predictable equilibrium. And it took a secular constitutional court, over the opposition of the All India Muslim Personal Law Board, to kill the trigger practice. Contrast Jesus: divorce concessions exist 'because of your hardness of heart' (Matthew 19:8-9), with no ritual requiring the woman's body as the price of reconciliation.

surah-9-missing-basmala.claim: Surah 9, al-Tawbah or Bara'ah, is the only one of 114 surahs lacking the bismillah heading. Asked why, Uthman explained in Jami at-Tirmidhi 3086 that al-Anfal came early in Medina and Bara'ah late, that its subject matter resembled al-Anfal's, and that the Prophet died without clarifying whether it was part of it. 'So I put them adjacent and did not write the basmala between them.' The caliph who standardised the Quran describes a surah boundary settled by his own inference, not by revelation.
surah-9-missing-basmala.response: The common devotional answer, surveyed at IslamQA 173672, is that the basmala, which is the mercy formula, was deliberately omitted because al-Tawbah opens with a declaration of war and the repudiation of treaties. A surah of the sword needs no invocation of mercy, a view attributed to Ali. Others hold that the surah order and boundaries were fixed by the Prophet's instruction, tawqifi. And Uthman's account is graded variously, with Darussalam calling it hasan while some later critics weaken it.
surah-9-missing-basmala.rationale: The two traditional answers undercut each other. If the omission were a revealed judgment about mercy and war, Uthman would not have explained it as his own uncertainty about where one surah ends and another begins. State the weakness plainly: the grading of Tirmidhi 3086 is contested, so use this as corroboration inside the compilation story rather than as your lead. This site's uthman-burning and compilation cases carry the primary weight. The undisputed core is untouched by the grading dispute.
