The basmala is missing, the companion codices ordered surahs differently, and the arrangement of the mushaf passed through editorial decisions made after Muhammad.

haman-in-pharaohs-egypt.claim: The Quran places a figure named Haman in Egypt as Pharaoh's officer at the time of Moses (28:6; 28:8; 28:38; 29:39; 40:24; 40:36-37). Pharaoh even asks Haman to fire bricks and build a lofty tower, so as to look upon the God of Moses. But Haman is the vizier of the Persian king in the book of Esther (3:1), set roughly a millennium after Moses. And the tower-to-heaven motif belongs to Babel (Genesis 11:3-4), where baked bricks are likewise specified. The Quran reads like a fusion of Esther's villain with the Babel story, relocated to Egypt — exactly the blend already circulating in Jewish midrashic storytelling.
haman-in-pharaohs-egypt.response: Two Muslim defences are offered. The first is that the Quranic Haman is simply a different Egyptian with a similar name. The second is the 'scientific miracle' version, popularised from Maurice Bucaille and developed by Islamic Awareness. The letters hmn-h appear in an Egyptian name catalogue, as a chief of stone-quarry workers, so on this reading the Quran preserves an authentic Egyptian name that history had lost.
haman-in-pharaohs-egypt.rationale: The hmn-h argument dissolves on inspection. It rests on reading a German-transliterated entry in a name lexicon. The reconstructed vowels are conjectural. No Egyptologist endorses 'Haman' as an Egyptian name. And the alleged quarry chief has no connection to Moses's era, or to a vizier's role. Meanwhile the academic treatment, by Adam J. Silverstein and published by Princeton and Oxford, concludes that both Hamans are the same folkloric villain, migrating between the Persian and Pharaonic courts through the fluidity of Near Eastern narrative. Silverstein is no Christian apologist. That frame concedes precisely what the dictation-from-heaven model cannot afford: the Quran inherited a literary character, complete with Babel's bricks and tower, and set him in the wrong court. It pairs naturally with this site's Samaritan-anachronism and Dhul-Qarnayn cases, as a third independent instance of the same pattern.

prophetic-medicine-science-test.claim: Dawah routinely claims that Muhammad's words anticipate modern science. The sahih medical corpus is the test. Dip the fly in your drink, because one wing carries the disease and the other its cure (Sahih al-Bukhari 3320). The tribesmen of Ukl and Urayna were prescribed camel milk and camel urine as medicine (Sahih al-Bukhari 233; 5686). And black seed is 'a healing for every disease except death' (Sahih al-Bukhari 5688). A source reliable enough to establish embryology miracles is reliable enough to own these.
prophetic-medicine-science-test.response: Three defences circulate. The first is vindication by study, citing a small 2021 Saudi-affiliated study on fly-wing dipping and assorted camel-urine papers as confirmation. The second is reclassification: prophetic medical statements are worldly opinion rather than revelation, following the date-pollination hadith, 'you know better the affairs of your world' (Sahih Muslim 2363). The third is that black seed's 'every disease' is idiomatic hyperbole for broad benefit. ICRAA and mainstream dawah treatments of the fly hadith set these out.
prophetic-medicine-science-test.rationale: The defences cannot all be held at once, and each costs something. The vindication studies are small, in fringe journals, and post hoc — and the WHO warns against consuming camel urine, which was a live issue during MERS. The worldly-opinion escape hatch contradicts how the statements are framed, as categorical claims about disease, delivered as authoritative teaching and preserved in the medicine chapters of the Sahih. And once 'every disease except death' is hyperbole, the method that finds precise embryology in equally loose language collapses. As a usage note, deploy this as a response when the scientific-miracles claim is made. As a cold-open attack it reads as mockery and closes the conversation.

adam-sixty-cubits.claim: Sahih al-Bukhari 3326 says: 'Allah created Adam, making him 60 cubits tall', which is roughly 27 to 30 metres, or 90 feet. It ends: 'people have been decreasing in stature since Adam's creation'. Sahih al-Bukhari 6227 and Sahih Muslim 2841 carry the report as well. Both clauses are empirically testable and false. No giant human remains exist, and the skeletal record runs the other way, since average stature has increased in recent centuries and no ancient population approached even three metres.
adam-sixty-cubits.response: IslamQA 22058 affirms the hadith literally and treats the fossil and archaeological objection as inconclusive. Others follow a suggestion that the sixty-cubit height applies to Adam in Paradise, or to people in Paradise, since 'whoever enters Paradise will be in the form of Adam', rather than to earthly humans. Notably, Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani had already flagged the problem in Fath al-Bari in the 15th century. He observed that the dwellings and remains of ancient nations do not indicate such heights, and confessed difficulty resolving it.
adam-sixty-cubits.rationale: The Paradise-only reading fails, because the hadith's closing line about mankind decreasing in stature 'until now' is explicitly about earthly history. And the greatest classical commentator on Bukhari conceded the empirical contradiction six centuries ago without answering it. The case's real payload is not the absurd image but the method. This is Bukhari, the collection billed as second only to the Quran, transmitting a checkable falsehood. That reframes every 'but it's sahih' appeal elsewhere, including on Aisha's age, the fly, and the sun's prostration. Keep it as a supporting case, not a lead.

aisha-was-19-revisionism.claim: A popular modern Muslim counter to the Aisha case runs as follows. The age-nine report comes from a single narrator, Hisham ibn Urwa, whose memory failed in Iraq. And calculations from his sister Asma's age — ten years older, and dead at 100 in 73 AH — put Aisha at 17 to 19 at consummation.
aisha-was-19-revisionism.response: The factual correction is supplied by Muslim scholarship itself. The age reports are not solitary. They come from Aisha in the first person through multiple independent chains, including al-Aswad and other students of Aisha besides Hisham's line, in both Bukhari and Muslim. So impugning Hisham's late-life memory removes nothing. The Asma calculation rests on a report by Ibn Abi al-Zinad, who was born decades after Asma's death, which is evidentially far weaker than the sahih chains it is invoked to overturn. The Yaqeen Institute and ICRAA, both mainstream Muslim institutions, defend age nine and label the 19 thesis methodological revisionism.
aisha-was-19-revisionism.rationale: This entry exists because you will hear the claim. It circulates widely in dawah despite being rejected by Islam's own hadith scholarship. The decisive move in conversation is not to argue the chains yourself, but to hand the Muslim their own institutions: Yaqeen's paper is literally titled 'The Age of Aisha: Rejecting Historical Revisionism and Modernist Presumptions'. A defence that orthodoxy itself refuses is worth noticing, and the reason for the refusal matters. Accepting it would concede that sahih-graded, multiply attested reports can be discarded when they are uncomfortable, which dismantles the hadith canon it is trying to protect. Pair this with the aisha-age case; it is that case's rebuttal shield.

avoid-muhammad-never-existed.claim: The loud version says Muhammad is a myth. On that story he was made up later, by Arabs building an empire, and there is no proof he ever lived. It was spread by Robert Spencer's book 'Did Muhammad Exist?' and by writers online.
avoid-muhammad-never-existed.response: The correction is that sources outside Islam name him within years of his death. The Doctrina Jacobi, from about 634 to 640, speaks of a prophet who has appeared among the Saracens. The Armenian chronicle put down to Sebeos, from the 660s, names him and tells of his preaching of one God. There are coins too, and inscriptions, and the Dome of the Rock. Then there is Patricia Crone. She was the best known of the doubters about Islam's origins, and the one critics love to quote. She said flatly that there is no doubt Muhammad lived, and called the early outside evidence irrefutable.
avoid-muhammad-never-existed.rationale: Here is why it backfires. Any Muslim who has read a little, or run one search, will hand you Crone's own words and the seventh-century sources. Then your standing on all the rest goes with it — Sanaa, the qira'at, the study of sources. You will have shown that you bend evidence to suit yourself. Say this instead. The man lived. The problem is his life story. The sira rests on sources put together 150 to 200 years later, and Ibn Ishaq only survives through Ibn Hisham's edition. That point is honest, and it does far more damage. This site's hadith-chain-of-custody case already makes it.

avoid-petra-qibla.claim: The loud version comes from Dan Gibson's book 'Early Islamic Qiblas'. It holds that the first mosques face Petra and not Mecca. On that story Petra was the holy city, the tradition moved it later, and the whole account of Islam's beginnings is made up.
avoid-petra-qibla.response: The correction comes from David A. King. He is the leading historian of how the qibla was worked out, and he wrote 'From Petra back to Makka' and 'The Petra Fallacy'. He showed that the method reads a modern skill into an old world. The first mosque builders had no way to take bearings across a curved earth. They lined up mosques by the sky as farmers see it — sunrise and sunset at the solstice, and the rising of stars. That is why the directions scatter. Take modern bearings and read them back into seventh-century building, and you will make a line to Petra appear. No academic historian of early Islam holds the thesis. That includes the doubters whom critics quote on other points.
avoid-petra-qibla.rationale: Here is why it backfires. The thesis is turned down not by Muslim apologists but by the very Western scholars this site leans on for Sanaa and the qira'at. Lean on Gibson and a ready friend answers with King. Your whole standard of evidence goes up in smoke. Say this instead: nothing is lost by dropping it. The problems on the record are stronger and undisputed. There is Uthman's burning, the companion codices, and how late the sira was written.

avoid-black-stone-worship-slogan.claim: The popular slogan says that Muslims claim to oppose idolatry but literally worship a black rock, bowing to it and kissing it.
avoid-black-stone-worship-slogan.response: The correction is that Islam's own canon pre-empts the charge. In Sahih al-Bukhari 1597, Umar kissed the Stone and said: 'I know that you are a stone and can neither benefit anyone nor harm anyone. Had I not seen Allah's Messenger kissing you, I would not have kissed you.' Muslims venerate the Stone in imitation of Muhammad while explicitly denying it any power. On their own definitions this is not worship, and prayer is directed toward the Kaaba as a direction, the qibla, not to it as an object.
avoid-black-stone-worship-slogan.rationale: Here is why it backfires. The Muslim answers with Umar's hadith in one sentence and wins the exchange. Worse, the charge invites a tu quoque about crosses, icons and relics, which drags the conversation into arguing about symmetry. What to say instead: this site's kaaba-black-stone-pagan-rites case asks the honest version of the question. Why did a religion founded on smashing paganism retain, unchanged, the pre-Islamic rites of circling a shrine and kissing a stone? Muslim sources document that continuity themselves, and Umar's own bewilderment underlines it. Origin, not worship, is the pressure point.

avoid-26-different-qurans.claim: The popular version, performed at Speakers' Corner by Jay Smith and Hatun Tash, waves a stack of printed Arabic Qurans: 'here are 26 different Qurans with 93,000 differences, and Muslims can't even tell you which one is preserved.'
avoid-26-different-qurans.response: The correction, conceded even in Muslim rebuttals of Smith, is that the printed editions are the canonical qira'at. These are transmitted reading traditions — Hafs, Warsh, Qalun, al-Duri and others — differing overwhelmingly in pronunciation and orthography, with a bounded set of wording variants, all descending from the Uthmanic consonantal skeleton. The 93,000 figure counts vowel and dialect differences. Calling them '26 different Qurans' is roughly like calling the KJV, NIV and ESV 'three different Bibles' — a framing Christians reject when Muslims use it, and should not use in reverse. Yasir Qadhi's treatment of the Quran's textual history gives the honest scholarly frame.
avoid-26-different-qurans.rationale: Here is why it backfires. A Muslim who has watched one rebuttal video explains the qira'at, the numbers deflate on inspection, and the audience concludes that the critic did not understand the material — squandering a real issue. What to say instead: this site already holds the strong version, in uthman-burning-companion-codices, sanaa-palimpsest-qiraat and uthman-standardization-qiraat. Why did preservation by Allah require Uthman to burn rivals? Why did Ibn Mas'ud reject surahs that are in today's mushaf? Which of the readings — differing in actual words, not just accent, as at Quran 2:184 — is the preserved dictation? Precision here wins; the stack of books loses. Note the asymmetry honestly: Islam claims letter-perfect dictation, so even small variants cut deeper against the Quran than against a Bible whose textual history is openly critical.

avoid-taqiyya-overclaim.claim: The loud version says taqiyya is a broad order for Muslims to lie to unbelievers. So nothing a Muslim says can be trusted. Not in talk, not in public life, not at an interfaith event.
avoid-taqiyya-overclaim.response: The correction is that taqiyya in the old law books is leave, not an order. It lets a man hide his faith under force, or when his life is at risk (Quran 16:106; 3:28's 'unless you fear them'). It was worked out mainly in Shia law, under Sunni attack. The base rule in Islam is that lying is a grave sin. What is really there is smaller, and on the record. Deceit is allowed in war — 'war is deceit' (Sahih al-Bukhari 3030). And there are cases such as the false words used in the killing of Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. That is what this site's taqiyya-deception case sets out.
avoid-taqiyya-overclaim.rationale: Here is why it backfires. The big claim cannot be tested. If every denial is itself taqiyya, then no evidence can ever count against you. People hear that move and stop weighing the rest of what you say. It also gets the rule wrong, and a Muslim can show you that in seconds. What to say instead is the small version. Islam lets a man hide his faith under threat. It allows deceit in war. And Muhammad did allow false words in one killing. That is on the record, it is damaging, and you can hold it. Telling the man in front of you that he is lying is unfair, and it ends the talk.

avoid-72-virgins-in-quran.claim: The popular version says that the Quran promises martyrs 72 virgins in paradise.
avoid-72-virgins-in-quran.response: The correction is that the number 72 appears nowhere in the Quran. The Quran promises houris — created, wide-eyed, virginal companions (56:22-24; 44:54; 55:56; 78:33) — without a count. The 72 figure is hadith. Jami at-Tirmidhi 1663 lists among the martyr's six rewards marriage to 'seventy-two wives from al-hur al-'ayn' — wives, not 'virgins', in the wording. It is graded sahih or hasan in mainstream collections, but it remains a hadith claim and not a Quranic one.
avoid-72-virgins-in-quran.rationale: Here is why it backfires. Say 'the Quran promises 72 virgins' and the Muslim truthfully replies 'no it doesn't'. You lose on a citation error, and the real point escapes with it. The substance survives precision. The Quran's paradise is explicitly material and sexual, which is this site's houris-material-paradise case, and the 72-wives detail for martyrs is in a sahih-graded hadith. Cite it as Tirmidhi 1663 and the technicality defence evaporates. Precision converts a losing slogan into an unanswerable citation.
